categories.H: Pain, return after pain and referral

syntheses.A: Across the twelve sources summarised so far, two findings are consistent. First, a previous running-related injury is the most reliably reported risk factor. It was identified in five of eight prospective cohorts reviewed by Saragiotto et al. (2014), with risk estimates between 1.7 and 2.7, and it was confirmed in the recreational cohort of Hespanhol Junior et al. (2013). Second, training parameters on their own do not show a consistent relationship with injury. The largest review in the list, covering 36 prospective studies and 23,047 runners, found conflicting evidence for weekly distance, duration, frequency, intensity and recent changes in training, and concluded that no universal progression rule, including the 10% rule, can be justified (Fredette et al., 2022). This agrees with the randomised trial of Buist et al. (2008) and the earlier review of Damsted et al. (2018). Evidence for sudden weekly increases is suggestive but inconsistent (Damsted et al., 2019), and the framework of Nielsen et al. (2018) explains why a single threshold is unlikely to fit all runners. The marathon cohort of McGrath et al. (2024) adds that more than four in ten runners reported an injury during a 16-week build, that overuse injuries accumulated as training progressed and that physiotherapy was the most commonly used form of care, while the review by Knechtle et al. (2026) links higher training volumes and lower preparation to injury in the same race. For trail and ultramarathon runners, the available data are mostly retrospective and cross-sectional, as shown by Hoffman and Krishnan (2014) and Viljoen et al. (2022), and the weakest source in this section is the review by Dempster et al. (2021). For the engine, these sources support using previous injury as a strong modifier of risk messaging, describing load-spike findings as associations rather than rules, monitoring more closely in the later weeks of a marathon block and building the main spike claim on the session-level Garmin-RUNSAFE findings already in the database.
syntheses.B: The five sources in this section agree on how training load should be measured, while they differ on how confidently it can be used to predict injury. There is broad agreement that external load, such as distance and pace from the watch, and internal load, such as heart rate and perceived effort, should be combined, and that a change in the relationship between the two may indicate fatigue, as described by Bourdon et al. (2017) and Halson (2014a). Session RPE offers a simple and valid way to capture internal load from a single post-session rating (Foster et al., 2001), and the runner's own report of how they feel responds to training load more sensitively and consistently than most objective markers (Saw et al., 2016). All sources also stress individual baselines rather than fixed population cut-offs. By contrast, the thresholds attached to the acute:chronic workload ratio and the recommendation to keep weekly increases below 10% come mainly from team sports and partly from unpublished data (Gabbett, 2016), and the consensus statement already notes that the ratio's validity has been questioned (Bourdon et al., 2017). For the engine, these sources support combining watch data with a short daily check-in and a post-run effort rating, comparing each runner with their own history, and treating any ratio-based spike threshold as an internal rule until the critique by Impellizzeri et al. (2020) has been reviewed.
syntheses.C: The six sources in this section agree on how HRV should be used, even though the evidence that HRV-guided training improves outcomes remains modest. First, single-day HRV values are unreliable, and both case data and re-analyses show that weekly or 7-day rolling averages of one vagal index, Ln rMSSD, give a more valid picture of training status (Plews et al., 2012, 2013, 2014). Second, at least 3 valid recordings per week are needed in trained athletes and about 5 in recreational runners (Plews et al., 2014). Third, HRV must be interpreted against the individual's own baseline and normal range, and a higher value is not automatically favourable, since HRV can rise during functional overreaching and can fall in elite athletes because of saturation rather than fatigue (Plews et al., 2013, 2014). The meta-analysis by Manresa-Rocamora et al. (2021) shows that HRV-guided training improves vagal HRV and may reduce the number of negative responders, but that its advantage for fitness and performance is small and not statistically significant. The recent perspective by Schaffarczyk and Sperlich (2026) adds that HRV responds to many stressors outside training and that the main gap is transparent decision rules rather than more data. The clinical review by Mendoza et al. (2026) offers a similar practical model but adds little for runners. For the engine, these sources support comparing a 7-day rolling HRV trend with the runner's own normal range, requiring a minimum number of valid nights before HRV influences the recommendation, and treating HRV as one input alongside the check-in rather than as a stand-alone readiness score.
syntheses.D: The four sources in this section describe how endurance training is distributed across intensities, although most of the evidence comes from elite or well-trained athletes. Descriptive data show that successful endurance athletes perform most of their training, roughly 80% of sessions, at low intensity and only a small share at threshold or high intensity (Seiler, 2010). Among elite distance runners, this distribution is usually pyramidal with meaningful threshold work, and it becomes more polarised close to competition, always within a hard-day, easy-day structure (Casado et al., 2022). In a 9-week randomised trial, a polarised programme improved laboratory markers of endurance more than high-volume, threshold or interval-only programmes (Stöggl & Sperlich, 2014), although none of these sources shows that one distribution is clearly best over the long term. A recent conference abstract adds that athletes asked to train easy without feedback drift into moderate intensity without noticing (Treff et al., 2026). For the engine, these sources support keeping most sessions genuinely easy, limiting hard sessions to about two or three per week, giving concrete heart-rate guidance for easy days, and classifying sessions by their main purpose rather than by minutes in each heart-rate zone. Transferring these elite-based patterns to recreational runners remains an assumption that the cards should state.
syntheses.E: The four sources summarised so far in this section concern how terrain and running technique change the load of a run. Slope alters running mechanics substantially, since downhill running increases impact forces, braking and tibial shock, whereas uphill running increases muscle work and metabolic cost, and runners' natural changes in pace on hills do not keep effort constant (Vernillo et al., 2017). Recent prediction equations can now estimate the metabolic cost of level, uphill and downhill running with reasonable accuracy for an average runner, and they clearly outperform the commonly used ACSM equation on slopes (Looney et al., 2026). However, metabolic cost and mechanical load diverge on descents, which are energetically cheap but mechanically demanding. Regarding technique, there is no evidence for a universally economical running style, and runners appear to self-optimise their stride with experience (Moore, 2016), while the only injury-related evidence on gait retraining here is a small uncontrolled poster (Martínez-Gramage et al., 2020). For the engine, these sources support grade-adjusting the load of hilly and trail runs, treating descent as a separate mechanical load signal rather than assuming that a low heart rate means an easy run, and avoiding prescriptive technique advice in runner-facing texts. Gottschall and Kram (2005) and Minetti et al. (2002), which underlie much of this evidence, are still to be reviewed.
syntheses.F: The two sources in this section come from the same research group and agree closely. Exercising in the heat raises heart rate and physiological strain and impairs endurance performance, particularly in people who are not yet acclimatised. Repeated exercise in the heat produces most adaptations within the first week, with near-complete adaptation after about 10 to 14 days, and the reduction in exercise heart rate is among the fastest adaptations to develop and to fade, as described by both Périard et al. (2015) and Racinais et al. (2015). The risk of heat illness appears highest early in summer and during sudden hot spells, and heat indices based on temperature alone can underestimate stress in humid or still conditions (Racinais et al., 2015). For the engine, these sources support a more cautious recommendation on the first hot days, interpreting a higher heart rate at a familiar pace in the heat as heat strain rather than lost fitness, and relaxing the heat adjustment gradually over about one to two weeks of repeated hot runs. Hydration advice should stay general, since the consensus also warns recreational athletes against overdrinking. The IOC consensus on sport events in the heat (Racinais et al., 2023) and the study by Ely et al. (2007) on weather and marathon performance are still to be reviewed.
syntheses.G: The five sources in this section agree that insufficient sleep impairs performance and recovery, but they differ greatly in quality. The strongest general reference is the joint consensus of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society, which recommends at least 7 hours of sleep per night for adults and links regularly shorter sleep to impaired performance, immune function and pain (Watson et al., 2015). For athletes, the review by Halson (2014b) shows that sleep loss affects prolonged submaximal exercise more than maximal efforts and that effects build up over consecutive nights, while a meta-analysis abstract finds higher injury odds in adolescents who chronically sleep poorly (Gao et al., 2019). The two broad narrative reviews by Kaczmarek et al. (2025) and Pyzik et al. (2026) add background but are too weak to support specific claims. For the engine, these sources support using repeated nights under 7 hours as a readiness signal, weighting a chronic sleep deficit more heavily than a single short night, and keeping supplement and medication suggestions out of the texts. The original cohort by Milewski et al. (2014), the review by Fullagar et al. (2015) and the athlete sleep consensus by Walsh et al. (2021) are still needed for runner-specific claims.
syntheses.H: The nine sources in this section define two different pain rules, a framework for returning after injury and a set of safety rules that override training advice. For tendon problems such as Achilles tendinopathy, continued running guided by pain of no more than 5 out of 10 during activity, pain that settles by the next morning and no week-to-week increase caused no harm compared with rest (Silbernagel et al., 2007), and allowing pain during rehabilitation exercise gave a small short-term benefit in chronic musculoskeletal pain (Smith et al., 2017). For bone stress injuries, by contrast, return to running is guided by no pain at all, and localised bone pain that persists after running, occurs during walking or appears at rest or at night signals the need for assessment (Warden et al., 2014). Return to sport is best seen as a continuum from participation to full performance, with clearance as a shared decision in which the clinician protects the athlete's health (Ardern et al., 2016). In addition, the international red-flag framework shows that single warning signs are weak on their own but that combinations, and above all signs of cauda equina syndrome, require urgent referral (Finucane et al., 2020). The critique by Jeukendrup et al. (2024) further shows that fatigue, illness and falling performance have many possible causes, which argues against the app naming any energy-deficiency condition. The reviews by Glisik and Frangež (2024), Toczyłowska et al. (2025) and Geworkian et al. (2026) add little and are methodologically weak. For the engine, these sources support keeping the rule that pain above 5 triggers a referral, adding bone-pain and red-flag symptoms that trigger a referral regardless of the pain score, treating clusters of fatigue, illness and performance decline as a referral signal rather than a diagnosis, and leaving clearance decisions to the physiotherapist. The IOC consensus on relative energy deficiency by Mountjoy et al. (2023) is still needed to balance the critique.
syntheses.I: The seven sources in this section address two separate questions, namely whether strength training prevents injury and whether it improves running performance. On injury, the meta-analysis by Lauersen et al. (2014) found that exercise-based prevention reduced sports injuries by about a third overall, that strength training had the largest effect and that stretching had none, although none of the strength trials involved runners. The editorial by Khan (2026) reports a similar pattern for warm-up programmes in young athletes. On performance, the evidence is more directly about runners. Adding strength training improved running economy by 2 to 8% without harming aerobic capacity or body composition (Blagrove et al., 2018), had a large effect on running economy in highly trained runners (Balsalobre-Fernández et al., 2016) and improved time-trial performance, most clearly with heavy loads or a combination of methods (Llanos-Lagos et al., 2024). Rønnestad and Mujika (2014) translate this into practical guidance of two sessions per week to build strength and about one session per week to maintain it. The quasi-experimental study by Yismaw et al. (2026) is consistent with these findings but too weak to cite. For the engine, these sources support an evidence card stating that two strength sessions per week make running more economical and lower the risk of injury, a maintenance mode of one session per week during race preparation, a prompt when no strength work has been logged for several weeks and a note that leg soreness is normal in the first weeks. Because evidence for injury prevention in runners specifically remains indirect, Toresdahl et al. (2020), the hip-strength trial by Toresdahl et al. (2025) cited in Knechtle et al. (2026) and Beattie et al. (2014) are still worth obtaining.

entries.apa: Buist, I., Bredeweg, S. W., van Mechelen, W., Lemmink, K. A. P. M., Pepping, G.-J., & Diercks, R. L. (2008). No effect of a graded training program on the number of running-related injuries in novice runners: A randomized controlled trial. The American Journal of Sports Medicine, 36(1), 33–39. https://doi.org/10.1177/0363546507307505

facts.Design: Randomised controlled trial (GRONORUN), 13-week follow-up, level 1 evidence
facts.Population: 532 novice runners aged 18 to 65 randomised and 486 analysed, with no regular running in the previous 12 months, preparing for a 4-mile (6.7 km) recreational event in Groningen, the Netherlands
facts.Exposure: Graded 13-week programme based on the 10% rule versus a standard 8-week programme, both with three run/walk sessions per week at a conversational pace
facts.Outcome: Running-related injury, defined as a musculoskeletal complaint of the lower extremity or back that restricted running for at least one week
facts.Main result: No difference in injury incidence (20.8% graded versus 20.3% standard, P = .90)

findings: Injury incidence was almost identical in the two groups, at 20.8% (52 of 250) in the graded programme and 20.3% (48 of 236) in the standard programme (χ² = 0.016, P = .90).
After adjustment for body mass index, the graded programme showed no significant protective effect (reported OR = 0.8, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.3), and survival curves did not differ (log-rank P = .18).
Injuries per 1,000 hours of running were 30 in the graded group and 38 in the standard group. The difference was not significant, and the authors note that the trial was not powered to detect it.
The lower leg (40%) and the knee (37%) were the most frequently injured sites.

New injuries peaked at a similar weekly running time in both groups, namely 44 minutes in week 5 of the graded programme and 46 minutes in week 2 of the standard programme. The authors report this descriptively and did not test it.
entries.relevance: This trial is the most direct test of the widely used 10% rule, and it did not show a benefit for novice runners. For the engine, a weekly increase below 10% should therefore not be presented to runners as an evidence-based safety threshold, and a load-progression card should state that a slower build-up alone did not reduce injuries in this population. The trial compared the average rate of progression over whole programmes, so it does not contradict the findings on sudden week-to-week or single-session jumps reported by Nielsen et al. (2014) and Schuster Brandt Frandsen et al. (2025).
entries.limits: The randomised design is a clear strength. However, participants were adults who had not run for at least a year and were training for a short 6.7 km event, so the results may not transfer to experienced runners. Load was prescribed in minutes, running intensity was not measured, both groups ran three times per week, and compliance reached only about two thirds of the prescribed volume. The authors themselves suggest that the contrast between the two programmes may have been too small to produce a difference. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for novice runners, low for other runner types.
entries.strength: moderate for novice runners, low for other runner types.

entries.apa: Damsted, C., Glad, S., Nielsen, R. O., Sørensen, H., & Malisoux, L. (2018). Is there evidence for an association between changes in training load and running-related injuries? A systematic review. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy, 13(6), 931–942. https://doi.org/10.26603/ijspt20180931

facts.Design: Systematic review of PubMed/Medline, SPORTDiscus, Embase and Scopus, searched to April 2017
facts.Studies included: 4 of 8,242 records (one randomised trial and three observational studies), runners aged 18 to 65
facts.Exposure: Change in training load, expressed as change in distance, volume, velocity or frequency
facts.Quality appraisal: Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and PEDro, with quality scores ranging from 22% to 100%
facts.Main conclusion: Very limited evidence that a sudden change in training load is associated with running-related injury

findings: Three of the four studies pointed toward higher injury risk after a sudden increase in load, whereas the randomised trial by Buist et al. (2008) found no difference between an average weekly increase of 10% and one of 24%.

The highest-quality study (Nielsen et al., 2014, quality score 100%) reported a hazard ratio of 1.59 (95% CI 0.96 to 2.66) for distance-related injuries when weekly distance increased by more than 30%, compared with a change of less than 10%. The confidence interval includes 1.

In another cohort (Nielsen et al., 2012), the increase in running distance in the week before injury was on average 86% larger than the weekly increase during other weeks (95% CI 12.9% to 159.9%, p = .026).
The authors conclude that no evidence supports the "10% rule" and that no well-defined threshold exists above which a sudden increase becomes hazardous.

They stress that relative change depends on the absolute baseline. An increase from 2 to 3 km per week is a 50% jump, whereas a runner covering 100 km per week who adds 3 km increases load by only 3%.
entries.relevance: This review sets the ceiling on how confidently the engine can speak about week-to-week increases. Load-spike cards should describe an association rather than a proven cause and should avoid naming a single safe percentage. The point about absolute versus relative change is directly relevant to the engine, because low-volume runners will often trigger large percentage changes from small absolute increases. The engine may therefore need a minimum absolute distance before a relative spike is flagged. This last suggestion is my own inference from the authors' argument and was not tested in the review.
entries.limits: Only four studies met the inclusion criteria, and they used different definitions of change and injury, some had short follow-up, and their quality varied widely. The search ended in April 2017, so the review predates the Garmin-RUNSAFE analyses (Schuster Brandt Frandsen et al., 2025), which should be read alongside it. Evidence strength for the card: low, useful mainly for the limits field.
entries.strength: low, useful mainly for the limits field.

entries.apa: Damsted, C., Parner, E. T., Sørensen, H., Malisoux, L., Hulme, A., & Nielsen, R. Ø. (2019). The association between changes in weekly running distance and running-related injury: Preparing for a half marathon. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy, 49(4), 230–238. https://doi.org/10.2519/jospt.2019.8541

facts.Design: Prospective cohort study (ProjectRun21), 14-week follow-up
facts.Population: 261 healthy recreational runners in Denmark aged 18 to 65, preparing for a half marathon, with a median weekly distance of 7 km (IQR 4 to 14)
facts.Exposure: Ratio of running distance in the current 7 days to the previous 7 days, recalculated after every session and grouped as a change under 20%, an increase of 20% to 60%, or an increase over 60%
facts.Data collection: Daily GPS watch or smartphone data and weekly injury questionnaires sent by email
facts.Outcome: Running-related injury according to the consensus definition (restriction of running for at least 7 days or 3 sessions, or consultation of a health professional)
facts.Main result: At day 21, the cumulative injury risk was 22.6 percentage points higher for increases of 20% to 60% than for changes under 20%

findings: 56 of 261 runners (21.5%) sustained a running-related injury during the 14 weeks.

At 21 days, runners who increased their weekly distance by 20% to 60% had a cumulative risk difference of 22.6% (95% CI 0.9% to 44.3%, P = .041) compared with runners who changed their distance by less than 20%.
The association was no longer significant at 56 and 98 days, and increases above 60% did not differ significantly from the reference group, so no dose-response relationship was confirmed.

The type of schedule (distance-based or pace-based) did not significantly modify the association. Nevertheless, about 30% more runners in the 20% to 60% state were injured on the distance-based schedule than on the pace-based schedule, which the authors treat as a hypothesis for future research.
entries.relevance: The exposure used here, a rolling 7-day distance divided by the previous 7 days and recalculated after each run, is close to what the engine can compute from daily Garmin data. The study therefore supports flagging a weekly increase of 20% to 60% as a period of elevated risk, particularly early in a build-up. At the same time, the missing dose-response and the loss of significance at later time points mean that a card should present this as a possible rather than a consistent association. The hint that runners on high-volume schedules may tolerate increases less well is too uncertain to drive a rule, although it fits the load-versus-capacity reasoning of Bertelsen et al. (2017).
entries.limits: The number of injuries per exposure group was small, which the authors flag as a risk of sparse-data bias. Runners chose their own schedule, weekly volumes were low, and distance rather than step count was used as the load measure. Evidence strength for the card: low to moderate, since the prospective design and objective GPS data are strengths but the estimates are imprecise.
entries.strength: low to moderate, since the prospective design and objective GPS data are strengths but the estimates are imprecise.

entries.apa: Dempster, J., Dutheil, F., & Ugbolue, U. C. (2021). The prevalence of lower extremity injuries in running and associated risk factors: A systematic review. Physical Activity and Health, 5(1), 133–145. https://doi.org/10.5334/paah.109

facts.Design: Systematic review following PRISMA, with three databases (ScienceDirect, PubMed and SPORTDiscus) searched on 20 November 2020 using a single search string
facts.Studies included: 24 original studies from 183 screened records, covering runners of all ages and levels
facts.Outcomes: Mean injury incidence overall and by sex, injury location, and reported risk factors
facts.Quality appraisal: No formal risk-of-bias or quality assessment is reported
facts.Main result: Mean incidence of lower extremity running injury of 37% (SD 11.8%), with the knee as the most common site
facts.Note: Not on the original download list and added in this batch

findings: The mean incidence of lower extremity running injuries across studies was 37% (SD 11.8%). Women showed a slightly higher mean incidence than men (39.7% versus 34.3%), but the difference was not statistically significant (P > .05).

The knee was the most commonly injured site (24.3% of injuries), followed by the calf or lower leg (15.9%) and the ankle or foot (15%). Among women the calf or lower leg was most affected, whereas among men it was the hip, pelvis or upper leg.
Risk factors reported in more than one study were less than 5 years of running experience, an injury in the previous 12 months, and running more than 3 times or more than 30 km per week.
The authors acknowledge that the sex-specific incidence figures were calculated separately from the location figures and therefore do not align with them.
entries.relevance: This review adds little that is not better supported elsewhere. Its main risk factors, previous injury and higher weekly exposure, match those of Saragiotto et al. (2014), which used a stricter design limited to prospective cohorts. For this reason, I would not cite it as the primary source on any card. At most, it could serve as a secondary reference for the typical anatomical distribution of running injuries.
entries.limits: Methodological quality is weak for a systematic review. The search relied on one search string in three databases, no risk-of-bias assessment is reported, and incidence values from studies with different injury definitions and follow-up periods were simply averaged. The abstract also states that women show a greater incidence, although the results report the difference as non-significant. Evidence strength for the card: very low.
entries.strength: very low.

entries.apa: Fredette, A., Roy, J.-S., Perreault, K., Dupuis, F., Napier, C., & Esculier, J.-F. (2022). The association between running injuries and training parameters: A systematic review. Journal of Athletic Training, 57(7), 650–671. https://doi.org/10.4085/1062-6050-0195.21

facts.Design: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42018112913) of MEDLINE, CINAHL, Embase and SPORTDiscus, searched to 7 July 2020
facts.Studies included: 36 studies (33 prospective cohorts and 3 randomised trials) with 23,047 runners
facts.Exposure: Weekly distance, duration, frequency and intensity, as well as recent changes in these parameters
facts.Quality appraisal: QualSyst, with 22 high, 5 good, 5 moderate and 4 low quality studies (median score 86.4%)
facts.Evidence grading: Strong, moderate, limited, very limited or conflicting, based on the number, quality, similarity and consistency of studies
facts.Main result: Conflicting evidence for every training parameter and for recent changes in training

findings: Overall, 26.2% of runners sustained an injury (range 8.8% to 91.3%), with 14.9% in novice, 26.1% in recreational and 62.6% in competitive runners. The knee (25.8%), foot and ankle (24.4%) and lower leg (24.4%) were the most frequently injured areas.

For weekly distance, eight studies suggested higher risk with greater distance, for example above 30 km per week (HR 3.28, 95% CI 1.23 to 8.75), whereas seven studies found no association. Evidence for duration, frequency and intensity was similarly split, and some high-quality studies even found that longer or more frequent running was associated with fewer injuries.

For recent changes in training, five of eleven studies linked a recent increase in distance to injury, five found no association and one reported mixed results, so the overall evidence was graded as conflicting.

The authors conclude that no universal recommendation on training parameters or progression can be issued and that the popular 10% rule is not justified. They attribute the conflicting findings mainly to inconsistent injury definitions (fewer than 40% of studies used a definition close to the consensus definition), follow-up periods ranging from 1 to 60 months, and the fact that only 5 of the 36 studies used GPS data.
entries.relevance: This is the most comprehensive review in the download list and the strongest source for the limits field of any card on training load. It confirms that no single distance, frequency or progression threshold is supported by the evidence, which means the engine's thresholds should be presented to runners as internal decision rules rather than scientific cut-offs. It also supports Došlap's reliance on objective watch data, since the authors name the lack of GPS-measured training as a main reason for the conflicting evidence. One detail to keep in mind is that the review describes the Buist et al. (2008) trial as a comparison of weekly distance progressions, whereas the trial itself prescribed minutes of running.
entries.limits: The review is large and preregistered, and it appraised study quality systematically, which makes it the strongest review in this section. However, heterogeneity prevented a meta-analysis, the search ended in July 2020 and therefore misses the Garmin-RUNSAFE analyses, and training parameters were examined in isolation rather than in interaction with individual factors. Evidence strength for the card: high confidence that the evidence is conflicting, which makes the source most useful for the limits field.
entries.strength: high confidence that the evidence is conflicting, which makes the source most useful for the limits field.

entries.apa: Hespanhol Junior, L. C., Pena Costa, L. O., & Lopes, A. D. (2013). Previous injuries and some training characteristics predict running-related injuries in recreational runners: A prospective cohort study. Journal of Physiotherapy, 59(4), 263–269. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1836-9553(13)70203-0

facts.Design: Prospective cohort study, 12-week follow-up with online surveys every two weeks
facts.Population: 200 recreational runners in São Paulo, Brazil, aged at least 18 with at least 6 months of running experience (191 analysed), with a median weekly distance of 28.5 km
facts.Exposure: Personal and training characteristics, including previous injury, session duration, speed training (short bouts of high-speed running), interval training (sessions alternating intensities, such as fartlek), surface and terrain
facts.Outcome: Self-reported running-related injury, defined as musculoskeletal pain attributed to running that prevented at least one training session
facts.Analysis: Generalised estimating equations, which account for repeated measurements and recurrent injuries
facts.Main result: Previous injury (OR 1.88) and speed training (OR 1.46) predicted injury, whereas interval training predicted lower risk (OR 0.61)

findings: 60 of 191 runners (31%) sustained 84 injuries during the 12 weeks, which corresponds to 10 injuries per 1,000 hours of running. Eighteen injured runners had two or more injuries, and five of these were recurrences.
Injuries lasted on average 3.4 weeks and had a mean pain intensity of 5.6 out of 10. Muscle injuries were the most common type (30%) and the knee was the most affected region (19%).

In the multivariable model, a previous running-related injury (OR 1.88, 95% CI 1.01 to 3.51) and speed training (OR 1.46, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.10) predicted injury. Session duration was also significant, although its effect was so small (OR 1.01, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.02) that the authors consider it irrelevant in practice.

Interval training was associated with lower injury risk (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.88). The authors explain this by the fact that recreational runners who do intervals usually alternate running with slower running or walking, which lowers the total intensity of the session. They also stress that these associations may not be causal.
entries.relevance: This study supports using a previous injury as a modifier that makes the engine's risk messaging more cautious, since it was the strongest predictor even over a short follow-up. The finding on speed training is relevant to how the engine explains higher-intensity sessions, although the opposite result for interval training suggests that the way intensity is structured may matter more than intensity itself. Because speed and interval training were broadly defined and self-reported, a card should present these findings as associations in recreational runners rather than as rules.
entries.limits: The prospective design and near-complete follow-up (96%) are strengths. However, injuries were self-reported without clinical confirmation, follow-up lasted only 12 weeks, and all runners came from the database of a single race organiser, which limits generalisability. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for previous injury, which agrees with other cohorts, and low for the training-type findings.
entries.strength: moderate for previous injury, which agrees with other cohorts, and low for the training-type findings.

entries.apa: Hoffman, M. D., & Krishnan, E. (2014). Health and exercise-related medical issues among 1,212 ultramarathon runners: Baseline findings from the Ultrarunners Longitudinal TRAcking (ULTRA) Study. PLoS ONE, 9(1), Article e83867. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0083867

facts.Design: Cross-sectional analysis of baseline enrolment data from a longitudinal cohort (ULTRA Study), with retrospective self-report of the previous 12 months
facts.Population: 1,212 active ultramarathon runners (median age 42.3 years, 68% men, 88% living in the United States), with a median running distance of 3,347 km in the previous year
facts.Outcomes: Chronic medical conditions, use of health care, exercise-related injuries and stress fractures in the previous 12 months
facts.Main result: 64.6% had an injury that caused at least one lost training day in the previous year, with a median of 14 lost days among those affected

findings: 77.0% of runners reported an exercise-related injury in the previous 12 months and 64.6% an injury that caused lost training, with a median of 14 lost training days among those affected. The knee was the most frequent site (24.0% of runners).
The annual incidence of stress fractures was 5.5%, and the foot was the most common location (44.5% of stress fractures). The authors link this to the greater demands of running on irregular terrain.

Injured runners were younger (mean 42.3 versus 44.7 years) and less experienced (15 versus 17 years of running and 5 versus 7 years of ultramarathon running) than uninjured runners. By contrast, their annual running distance (3,347 versus 3,413 km) and their share of running on concrete or asphalt did not differ.

Injured runners also spent a larger share of their exercise time at high intensity, a smaller share of their exercise time running, and were more likely to do regular resistance training. Runners with a stress fracture were more often women, had run a greater distance in the past year and more often had a previous stress fracture.
Serious chronic conditions were uncommon, whereas allergies (25.1%) and exercise-induced asthma (13.0%) were more common than in the general population.
entries.relevance: This source is relevant for Došlap users who run ultramarathons or long trail races. Among these experienced runners, total annual distance did not distinguish injured from uninjured runners, whereas less running experience did, which fits the load-versus-capacity view that runners who have adapted over many years tolerate high volumes better. The findings on stress fractures, particularly the role of a previous stress fracture, female sex and higher annual distance, are useful for a referral-related card in Section H. The source is also relevant to Sections E and I.
entries.limits: The data are retrospective, self-reported and cross-sectional, so they describe associations at one point in time and cannot establish cause. The link between resistance training and more injuries may run in the opposite direction, since runners may start strength work after being injured. This is my own interpretation and is not stated by the authors. The sample consists of runners who had continued ultrarunning, and the authors themselves note that favourable characteristics may have allowed these individuals to keep participating. Evidence strength for the card: low.
entries.strength: low.

entries.apa: Knechtle, B., Thuany, M., Nikolaidis, P. T., Forte, P., Leite, L. B., Lepers, R., Chlíbková, D., Weiss, K., Rosemann, T., Vancini, R. L., & Duric, S. (2026). The New York City Marathon: A systematic review of performance, participation, pacing, and health-related outcomes. EXCLI Journal, 25, 591–620. https://doi.org/10.17179/excli2026-9354

facts.Type: Systematic review with narrative synthesis
facts.Sample: 76 publications on the New York City Marathon, searched up to February 2026
facts.Domains: Participation, performance, age, nationality, pacing, environmental conditions, injuries and medical aspects
facts.Note: Not on the original download list. The DOI is printed in the PDF but was not yet registered in Crossref at the time of checking

findings: About 10% of runners had a major injury that prevented them from starting or finishing, and higher training volumes were consistently associated with more injuries.
Having completed a half marathon beforehand and a longer longest training run were associated with fewer race-day injuries, based on the studies by Toresdahl and colleagues.
Higher temperatures slowed performance more than course factors did, particularly among slower runners.
Most runners paced positively, with the slowest split between 35 and 40 km, and older and faster runners paced more evenly.
entries.relevance: The review is mainly useful as a map of the New York City Marathon cohort studies. It points to a newer trial by Toresdahl et al. (2025) in which a hip-focused strength programme was associated with a 64% lower risk of overuse injury, which I have not verified and which would be worth downloading for Section I. The heat and pacing findings are consistent with Section F.
entries.limits: The review covers a single race, synthesises heterogeneous studies narratively and does not assess study quality in a way that allows pooled estimates. It should be cited only for descriptive context, and the individual primary studies should be used for evidence cards.

entries.apa: McGrath, T. M., Fontana, M. A., & Toresdahl, B. G. (2024). Injury patterns and healthcare utilisation by runners of the New York City Marathon. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine, 10(1), Article e001766. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjsem-2023-001766

facts.Design: Secondary analysis of a 16-week prospective observational cohort
facts.Participants: 1,049 runners training for the New York City Marathon
facts.Data: Injury surveys every 4 weeks, one week before and one week after the race, covering location, diagnosis, onset and treatment
facts.Note: Not on the original download list. It uses the same cohort programme as Toresdahl et al. (2020), which is still on the list

findings: Overall, 42.6% of runners reported an injury, 38.4% during training and 14.1% during the race.

Foot, knee and hip injuries were most common during training, most injuries affected muscle, tendon, fascia or bursa, and the share of overuse injuries grew as training progressed while acute injuries stayed constant.
Half of the injured runners (50.1%) sought medical care, and physiotherapy was the most common type of care (11.1% of runners during training).
About 1 in 23 runners had an MRI during training or after the race.
entries.relevance: This source is useful both for the engine and for the business plan. For the engine, it supports a card explaining that overuse injuries build up during a marathon block, which justifies closer monitoring in the later weeks. For the business plan, it provides evidence that injured runners use physiotherapy more than any other form of care, which supports the Došlap model of connecting runners with physiotherapists.
entries.limits: Injuries were self-reported and not clinically confirmed, the sample consisted of a single large-city marathon population in the United States, and healthcare use may differ in the Czech system. It is descriptive and does not identify causes.

entries.apa: Nielsen, R. O., Bertelsen, M. L., Møller, M., Hulme, A., Windt, J., Verhagen, E., Mansournia, M. A., Casals, M., & Parner, E. T. (2018). Training load and structure-specific load: Applications for sport injury causality and data analyses. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 52(16), 1016–1017. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2017-097838

facts.Type: Editorial (conceptual paper without new data), externally peer reviewed
facts.Core concepts: Training load, structure-specific cumulative load and structure-specific load capacity
facts.Main message: Change in training load should be the primary exposure in studies of injury causes, while body, technique, surface and capacity variables should be treated as effect-measure modifiers
facts.Version note: The downloaded PDF is the Online First version from July 2017. The final version appeared in 2018, 52(16), 1016–1017, and is the one to cite.

findings: Training load is defined as a measurable volume such as step count, distance run or time spent training. Changes in it over time, for example week-to-week change or the acute:chronic workload ratio, are used as time-varying exposures.
Structure-specific cumulative load is the sum of the per-step loads that a given tissue receives during a session. It cannot be measured directly in large studies, so proxy variables are needed.

Magnitude-related variables such as body weight and vertical movement change how much load each step produces, while distribution-related variables such as equipment, technique and surface change where that load goes. The authors use rearfoot versus forefoot striking as an example.

Capacity-related variables, including previous or current injury, time between sessions, strength and diet, determine how much load a structure can withstand. Injury occurs when structure-specific load exceeds structure-specific capacity.
Some modifiers, such as surface, terrain and vertical movement, change within a single session, which may require calculating a session-specific load.
entries.relevance: This paper provides the conceptual justification for the engine's load-versus-capacity quadrant. It supports treating distance or time as the core load signal and using terrain, body mass and previous injury as modifiers of that signal rather than as independent risk scores. Its emphasis on within-session variation also supports analysing individual sessions, which aligns with the single-session approach of Schuster Brandt Frandsen et al. (2025). Because it is an editorial without data, it should support an explanatory card on why the same distance loads runners differently, not a card that states an effect size. It is also relevant to Section B.
entries.limits: Expert opinion, which is the lowest level of evidence. The paper offers a framework and analytical recommendations but no quantitative thresholds. Evidence strength for the card: conceptual framework only.
entries.strength: conceptual framework only.

entries.apa: Saragiotto, B. T., Yamato, T. P., Hespanhol Junior, L. C., Rainbow, M. J., Davis, I. S., & Lopes, A. D. (2014). What are the main risk factors for running-related injuries? Sports Medicine, 44(8), 1153–1163. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-014-0194-6

facts.Design: Systematic review restricted to prospective cohort studies, six databases searched to December 2012
facts.Studies included: 11 prospective cohorts with 4,671 pooled participants, in which 60 different risk factors were investigated
facts.Quality appraisal: Adapted Newcastle-Ottawa-type scale, with most studies scoring at least 9 of 12 stars
facts.Synthesis: Narrative, because heterogeneous statistical methods prevented a meta-analysis
facts.Main result: A previous injury in the last 12 months was the most consistent risk factor

findings: A previous injury, usually within the last 12 months, was a risk factor in 5 of the 8 studies that examined it, with risk estimates between 1.7 and 2.7.

A weekly distance above 64 km was a risk factor in 2 of 5 studies, a higher Q angle in 2 of 3 studies, and weekly running frequency in 2 of 5 studies. The direction of the frequency finding differed between studies, since one found running once a week to be a risk factor for women.
Sex was not associated with injury in most of the studies.
Only one study used random sampling and only six had a follow-up of at least 6 months. Ascertainment of exposure and assessment of outcome were the weakest quality criteria.
The authors suggest that a previous injury may raise risk either because the earlier injury had not fully healed or because runners change their movement pattern to protect the injured area.
entries.relevance: This review is the strongest source so far for the claim that a previous injury increases the risk of a new one, and it supports treating injury history as an input that makes the engine more conservative. Its findings on training variables are weak and partly inconsistent, so they should not drive engine rules. The 64 km threshold in particular comes from only two studies and concerns mainly high-volume runners.
entries.limits: Restricting the review to prospective cohorts is a strength. However, only 11 studies were available, no meta-analysis was possible, the search ended in 2012, and exposure and outcome assessment were weak in most studies. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for previous injury, low for training variables. A different 2014 paper by Saragiotto and colleagues, on what runners believe about injury risk, is already in your database and should not be confused with this one.
entries.strength: moderate for previous injury, low for training variables. A different 2014 paper by Saragiotto and colleagues, on what runners believe about injury risk, is already in your database and should not be confused with this one

entries.apa: Viljoen, C., Janse van Rensburg, D. C. C., van Mechelen, W., Verhagen, E., Silva, B., Scheer, V., Besomi, M., Gajardo-Burgos, R., Matos, S., Schoeman, M., Jansen van Rensburg, A., van Dyk, N., Scheepers, S., & Botha, T. (2022). Trail running injury risk factors: A living systematic review. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 56(10), 577–587. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2021-104858

facts.Design: Living systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42021240832), eight databases searched to 18 March 2021, with updates planned every 6 months for at least 5 years
facts.Studies included: 19 studies, of which 10 examined risk factors in 2,785 participants
facts.Population: Trail runners, defined as running on natural surfaces with less than 20% on paved surfaces, from submarathon to multiday ultramarathon distances
facts.Study quality: Mean quality score of 66.7%, mostly cross-sectional designs with univariate analyses, and 80.8% of participants were men
facts.Main result: Eight intrinsic and nine extrinsic factors associated with injury, each reported in single studies and not replicated

findings: Factors reported as associated with higher injury risk were more running experience (over 6 years), being a 'level A' runner, a higher score on the propensity to sports accident questionnaire (PAD-22), neglecting a warm-up, not using a specialised running plan, regular training on asphalt, double training sessions per day and physical labour occupations.

Muscle cramping in a 161 km race was associated with a history of cramping, post-race markers of muscle damage and a slower finishing time. Sunburn was associated with more than 3 hours of training per day, relying on shade as the main sun protection, younger age, low skin phototype and being single.

Injury incidence ranged from 0.7 to 61.2 injuries per 1,000 hours of running and prevalence from 1.3% to 90%. The two prospective training studies reported 10.7 injuries per 1,000 hours and a prevalence of 22.4% to 52%, which the authors note is similar to other running literature.

The foot and toe were the most commonly injured areas, followed by the ankle and the hip or groin. Blisters, joint sprains and tendinopathies were the most common pathology types, and the ankle was reported more often than the knee, which the authors link to uneven trail surfaces.
entries.relevance: This is the only systematic synthesis of trail-specific injury risk in the download list, and it gives useful context for trail runners using Došlap, especially the prominence of ankle sprains and foot blisters on technical terrain. However, the authors themselves restrict the clinical use of the risk factors because they come mostly from small, retrospective, cross-sectional studies. For this reason, I would not use any single risk factor from this review as an engine trigger. The review is better suited to a context card describing the typical injury profile in trail running. Because it is a living review, a later update may exist and should be checked before the card is finalised. It is also relevant to Section E.
entries.limits: Overall certainty is low. Several factors listed as significant come from one Greek study of 40 runners with self-reported injuries, and the review reports p-values above .05 for some of them (not using a specialised running plan p = .0995, double sessions per day p = .06, level A runner p = .067, physical labour p = .058) while still describing them as significant. This inconsistency should be kept in mind when writing the card. Race-based studies focused mainly on ultramarathons, which may overstate the share of blisters, and findings may transfer poorly to women. Evidence strength for the card: very low for individual risk factors, low to moderate for the descriptive injury profile.
entries.strength: very low for individual risk factors, low to moderate for the descriptive injury profile.

entries.apa: Bourdon, P. C., Cardinale, M., Murray, A., Gastin, P., Kellmann, M., Varley, M. C., Gabbett, T. J., Coutts, A. J., Burgess, D. J., Gregson, W., & Cable, N. T. (2017). Monitoring athlete training loads: Consensus statement. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 12(Suppl. 2), S2-161–S2-170. https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2017-0208

facts.Type: Consensus statement from an expert conference ('Monitoring Athlete Training Loads: The Hows and the Whys', Doha, February 2016)
facts.Authors: 11 sport scientists and practitioners, including Gabbett, Coutts and Kellmann
facts.Scope: Definitions of internal and external load, measurement methods across sports, analysis models, the link between load and injury, and the future of monitoring
facts.Main message: Internal and external load should be combined, monitoring should be individualised, and no single measure can accurately quantify fitness and fatigue or predict performance

findings: Internal load is defined as the relative physiological and psychological stress imposed on the athlete (for example heart rate, lactate or RPE), and external load as the work performed, measured independently of internal load (for example speed, distance, power or GPS data).

The two should be used together, because the same external session can produce a different internal load depending on fatigue, emotional state, recent training or illness. A higher internal load for a standard external load may indicate fatigue or reduced fitness, while a lower one suggests the athlete is coping and gaining fitness.
Psychological measures are described as more sensitive and consistent than physiological indicators in overtraining studies, and they can be reported within minutes rather than days.

The ACWR is described as a simplification of Banister's fitness-fatigue model. The statement reports its association with injury in team sports but also notes that its validity has been questioned because rolling averages ignore the decaying effect of past load. An exponentially weighted moving average is suggested as an alternative, although further research is needed.

Fitness-fatigue and neural-network models are judged to be of little practical benefit for predicting individual performance, while the statement also notes that undertraining and 'troughs' in load may be as harmful as 'spikes'.
entries.relevance: This statement supports the engine's core design of combining watch data (external load) with heart rate and subjective check-ins (internal load). The idea that a rising heart rate or effort at a familiar pace can signal fatigue is directly usable as a readiness signal, provided pace, terrain and weather are controlled for, which the authors themselves stress. The critical remarks on the ACWR and the suggestion to use exponentially weighted averages are relevant if the engine uses a ratio of recent to chronic load. The statement's caution that no single metric predicts performance also supports how the AI texts should present the engine's recommendations.
entries.limits: This is an expert consensus rather than a systematic review, and it focuses mainly on elite sport. Several authors, including Gabbett, are closely associated with the ACWR. Evidence strength for the card: moderate as a framework for combining internal and external load, low for any specific threshold.
entries.strength: moderate as a framework for combining internal and external load, low for any specific threshold.

entries.apa: Foster, C., Florhaug, J. A., Franklin, J., Gottschall, L., Hrovatin, L. A., Parker, S., Doleshal, P., & Dodge, C. (2001). A new approach to monitoring exercise training. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 15(1), 109–115. https://doi.org/10.1519/00124278-200102000-00019

facts.Design: Two-part validation study comparing the session RPE method with a heart-rate-based reference method
facts.Participants: Part 1: 12 recreational-level, well-trained cyclists (6 men, 6 women). Part 2: 14 players from a collegiate men's basketball team
facts.Method tested: Session RPE: about 30 minutes after a session, the athlete rates its overall difficulty on a modified 0 to 10 category-ratio scale, and this rating is multiplied by session duration in minutes
facts.Reference method: Summated heart-rate zone score, in which minutes in five zones (50% to 100% of peak heart rate) are weighted 1 to 5 and summed
facts.Sessions: Steady-state cycling of 30, 60 and 90 minutes, five interval formats at the same mean power, and basketball practice and games
facts.Main result: Session RPE scores were consistently higher in absolute terms but followed the heart-rate method closely and consistently across very different types of exercise
facts.Note: The downloaded PDF is a scanned copy with imperfect text recognition, so figures were checked against the readable tables.

findings: Across steady-state exercise, interval exercise and basketball, the session RPE method produced a consistent relationship with the summated heart-rate zone method, and the regression lines for the two very different groups nearly overlapped.

In absolute terms, session RPE gave significantly higher scores than the heart-rate method for most sessions (for example, 744 versus 652 units for basketball and 432 versus 350 units for 90 minutes of steady cycling). The authors argue that this is expected, because the heart-rate method caps intensity at five zones.

The authors conclude that session RPE is a valid way to quantify training across a wide variety of exercise, including high-intensity intervals where heart rate works less well, and that it does not require knowledge of maximal heart rate.

From daily session RPE loads, the authors derive weekly load as well as training 'monotony' (mean daily load divided by its standard deviation) and 'strain' (weekly load multiplied by monotony), which they suggest may indicate the likelihood of negative training outcomes.
In the authors' experience, most athletes can use the method with minimal instruction, typically by answering the question 'How was your workout?'
entries.relevance: Session RPE is the simplest way for the engine to capture internal load, since it only needs one rating per session combined with the duration that Garmin already records. It directly supports adding a post-run effort rating to the check-in and combining it with watch data. The method is also useful where heart rate is unreliable, for example during short intervals or on technical terrain. The concepts of monotony and strain could inform the weekly summary, although this paper proposes them without testing whether they predict injury or illness.
entries.limits: The samples were small and did not include runners, and the comparison was with another load estimate rather than with an injury or performance outcome. The paper shows that session RPE tracks heart-rate load, not that it prevents injury. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for session RPE as a valid measure of internal load, very low for monotony and strain as warning signals.
entries.strength: moderate for session RPE as a valid measure of internal load, very low for monotony and strain as warning signals.

entries.apa: Gabbett, T. J. (2016). The training–injury prevention paradox: Should athletes be training smarter and harder? British Journal of Sports Medicine, 50(5), 273–280. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2015-095788

facts.Type: Narrative review presenting a conceptual model, single author
facts.Evidence base: Mainly team-sport studies (rugby league, rugby union, Australian football, cricket), partly supplemented by unpublished data from the author's own work
facts.Main message: Athletes accustomed to high training loads have fewer injuries, and non-contact injuries are more likely caused by excessive and rapid increases in load than by training itself
facts.Key metric: Acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR), with about 0.8 to 1.3 described as a 'sweet spot' and 1.5 or more as a 'danger zone'
facts.Version note: The downloaded PDF is the Online First version from January 2016. The final version is 50(5), 273–280, and is the one to cite.

findings: The paper proposes the 'training-injury prevention paradox', whereby athletes accustomed to high training loads have fewer injuries than athletes training at lower loads. Appropriately graded hard training is presented as protective because it develops physical qualities associated with lower injury risk.
Both too little and too much training are described as raising injury risk, a U-shaped relationship reported in cricket fast bowlers and also in baseball and rugby union.

Based on unpublished modelling of the author's own data, injury risk was below 10% when weekly load stayed between 5% less and 10% more than the previous week, but rose to between 21% and 49% when load increased by 15% or more. On this basis, the author recommends limiting weekly increases to less than 10%.

Acute load is defined as the load of roughly the last week and chronic load as the rolling average of the last 3 to 6 weeks. In cricket fast bowlers, an ACWR of 1.5 or more was followed by a 2 to 4 times greater injury risk in the next 7 days. Drawing on cricket, Australian football and rugby league, the author presents 0.8 to 1.3 as a low-risk range.
The author himself cautions that load-injury relationships may differ between sports and that applying these thresholds to athletes in individual sports should be done with caution.
entries.relevance: This paper is the origin of two ideas the engine may draw on, namely that chronic load protects as well as endangers, and that recent load relative to longer-term load matters more than either on its own. The protective role of chronic load fits the engine's load-versus-capacity logic and supports messages that encourage consistent training rather than simply cutting load. However, its specific thresholds should not be imported directly into Došlap. The recommendation of less than 10% per week rests on unpublished team-sport data and conflicts with the running-specific evidence in Section A, notably Buist et al. (2008) and Fredette et al. (2022). The ACWR itself has since been criticised on conceptual and statistical grounds, so the critique by Impellizzeri et al. (2020) should be read before any ACWR-based card is written.
entries.limits: This is a narrative review and expert opinion by the author who popularised the ACWR, and it relies largely on team sports and partly on unpublished data. None of the cited evidence comes from recreational runners. Evidence strength for the card: low for the specific thresholds, moderate for the general principle that well-prepared athletes tolerate load better.
entries.strength: low for the specific thresholds, moderate for the general principle that well-prepared athletes tolerate load better.

entries.apa: Halson, S. L. (2014a). Monitoring training load to understand fatigue in athletes. Sports Medicine, 44(Suppl. 2), 139–147. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-014-0253-z

facts.Type: Narrative review, single author (Australian Institute of Sport), open access
facts.Scope: External and internal load measures, markers of fatigue, current monitoring practice, individualisation and how to judge meaningful change
facts.Main message: Very few load and fatigue markers have strong scientific support, no single definitive marker exists, and monitoring should be individualised
facts.Citation note: Because Halson has a second 2014 paper in Section G, this one is cited as 2014a and the sleep review as 2014b.

findings: External load is the work completed by the athlete, whereas internal load is the athlete's physiological and perceptual response. A dissociation between the two may reveal the athlete's state of fatigue.

Session RPE (RPE on a 1 to 10 scale multiplied by session duration) is described as simple, valid and reliable, with individual correlations with heart-rate-zone scores of 0.75 to 0.90, although adding heart rate may explain some of the variance it misses.

Heart rate can vary by up to 6.5% from day to day at submaximal intensity, so hydration, environment and medication should be controlled for. Heart rate recovery may track training status, although findings on overreaching are conflicting.

Findings on HRV are inconsistent because of differing methods and high day-to-day variability. Weekly or 7-day rolling averages are suggested to be more valid than single-day values, with Ln rMSSD as the preferred index.

Biochemical, hormonal and immune markers are not currently justified for routine monitoring, whereas simple questionnaires and sleep diaries or actigraphy are considered useful. The author also warns against arbitrary cut-offs such as a change greater than 5%, and recommends judging change against each measure's typical error and smallest worthwhile change.
entries.relevance: This review supports several of the engine's design choices at once. It justifies using session RPE alongside watch data, interpreting HRV as a rolling average rather than a single morning value, and comparing each runner against their own baseline rather than against fixed population thresholds. The warning about day-to-day heart-rate variation and environmental influences is also relevant to how the engine interprets heart rate on hot days or hilly terrain. The HRV points should be linked to Plews et al. (2013) in Section C, which the review cites.
entries.limits: This is a narrative review without systematic search or quality appraisal, written mainly from the perspective of elite sport. Its recommendations reflect expert judgement rather than tested effects on injury or performance. Evidence strength for the card: moderate as a supporting reference for monitoring principles, low as a sole source.
entries.strength: moderate as a supporting reference for monitoring principles, low as a sole source.

entries.apa: Saw, A. E., Main, L. C., & Gastin, P. B. (2016). Monitoring the athlete training response: Subjective self-reported measures trump commonly used objective measures: A systematic review. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 50(5), 281–291. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2015-094758

facts.Design: Systematic review of Academic Search Complete, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus and PubMed, searched in May 2014
facts.Studies included: 56 original studies of athletes reporting concurrent subjective and objective measures of well-being
facts.Subjective: Mainly the Profile of Mood States (POMS), the
facts.measures: indices, oxygen uptake and performance tests
facts.Objective: Blood markers, hormones, immune markers, heart rate
facts.Main result: Subjective measures reflected acute and chronic training load with greater sensitivity and consistency than objective measures, and the two generally did not correlate
facts.Version note: The downloaded PDF is the Online First version from September 2015. The final version is 50(5), 281–291.

findings: Subjective well-being was typically impaired after an acute increase in training load and with ongoing chronic training, whereas an acute decrease in training load improved it.
Where subjective and objective measures differed within the same study (46% of studies), 85% of these differences favoured the subjective measures.
Objective measures were generally unresponsive to acute changes in load, with only creatine kinase and performance tests showing a typical response to both increases and decreases.

Individual subscales were more sensitive than total scores. For monitoring acute well-being, the authors suggest items on vigour or motivation, physical symptoms or injury, non-training stress, fatigue, physical recovery, general health and being in shape, and they note that sleep, irritability, willingness to train and how training felt may also be useful.
The authors conclude that subjective measures may stand alone or be combined with objective measures, since the two appear to capture different aspects of the athlete's state.
entries.relevance: This review provides the strongest justification in the list for giving the runner's own check-in real weight in the engine's readiness assessment, rather than relying on watch data alone. It also suggests which items a short daily check-in should contain, such as fatigue, muscle soreness or symptoms, motivation, stress outside training and sleep. Because single subscales were more informative than total scores, the engine may benefit from keeping check-in items separate rather than collapsing them into one number. This last point is my own inference applied to the engine and was not tested in the review.
entries.limits: The included studies were small and heterogeneous, used different questionnaires and timeframes, and mostly involved elite or highly trained athletes. The objective measures were largely laboratory and blood markers, so the review does not directly compare check-ins with wearable metrics such as HRV. In one place the results section states that well-being improved with an acute increase in load, which contradicts the abstract and discussion and is probably an error in the text. Evidence strength for the card: moderate.
entries.strength: moderate.

entries.apa: Manresa-Rocamora, A., Sarabia, J. M., Javaloyes, A., Flatt, A. A., & Moya-Ramón, M. (2021). Heart rate variability-guided training for enhancing cardiac-vagal modulation, aerobic fitness, and endurance performance: A methodological systematic review with meta-analysis. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 18(19), Article 10299. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph181910299

facts.Design: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of Web of Science, PubMed and Embase, searched to October 2020
facts.Studies included: 8 studies with 10 analysis units (7 randomised), 199 participants (106 HRV-guided, 93 predefined), ranging from sedentary adults to high-level athletes and including two groups of runners
facts.Comparison: Training adjusted day to day according to HRV versus a predefined training plan
facts.Risk of bias: Unclear to high for selection and detection bias, since most studies did not report how randomisation was done and only one blinded its assessors
facts.Main result: A small significant advantage for vagal HRV (SMD 0.50) and small, non-significant advantages for fitness and performance (SMD 0.20 to 0.26)

findings: HRV-guided training improved vagal-related HRV more than predefined training (SMD 0.50, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.91), but not resting heart rate (SMD 0.04).

For maximal aerobic capacity (SMD 0.20, 95% CI −0.07 to 0.47), capacity at the second ventilatory threshold (SMD 0.26, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.57) and endurance performance (SMD 0.20, 95% CI −0.09 to 0.48), effects consistently favoured HRV-guided training but were small and not statistically significant. No heterogeneity was found for these outcomes.

Individual responses were more uniform with HRV guidance. In one running study, VO₂max fell in 1 runner after HRV-guided training (11.1%) versus 4 runners after predefined training (50.0%), and in one cycling study performance declined in 14.3% versus 37.5% of athletes.

The studies differed in method. Some compared single daily values with a rolling reference of about 10 values, whereas others compared rolling averages with a fixed 3- to 4-week baseline. Rolling averages lead to fewer training changes, and it remains unclear which approach works better.
The authors conclude that HRV-guided training may maintain and improve vagal HRV with less likelihood of negative responses, but that any group-level advantage for fitness and performance is small.
entries.relevance: This is the best available estimate of what HRV guidance actually achieves, and it sets realistic expectations for how Došlap describes its readiness logic. Cards should present HRV guidance as a way to lower the chance of responding badly to training, rather than as a way to gain fitness faster. The comparison of daily and rolling approaches is directly relevant to the engine's design, even though the review cannot say which is better. This is the source to cite for the meta-analytic figures quoted by Schaffarczyk and Sperlich (2026).
entries.limits: Only 8 small studies were available, with mixed populations, inconsistent methods, short interventions and unclear to high risk of bias. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for the claim that group-level benefits are small or absent, low for the claim of fewer negative responders, which rests on a few individual studies.
entries.strength: moderate for the claim that group-level benefits are small or absent, low for the claim of fewer negative responders, which rests on a few individual studies.

entries.apa: Mendoza, M. F., Anzelmo, M. A., Rojas, A. A., Suan, N. M., & Lavie, C. J. (2026). Exercise training and heart rate variability: A guided optimization of cardiorespiratory fitness in cardiometabolic disease. Current Atherosclerosis Reports, 28(1), Article 77. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11883-026-01439-7

facts.Type: Narrative review in a cardiology journal
facts.Population focus: People with cardiometabolic disease (type 2 diabetes, obesity and metabolic syndrome), not athletes
facts.Scope: Cardiorespiratory fitness, aerobic and resistance training, HRV-guided training and consumer wearables (Garmin, Apple Watch, WHOOP, Oura, Polar)
facts.Note: Published in 2026 and not on the original download list. Its metadata were verified through Crossref.

findings: The review proposes a three-step HRV-guided model. First, a baseline is established from 7 to 14 days of near-daily recordings. Second, daily morning HRV is compared with the individual's rolling average and normal range. Third, high-intensity or threshold sessions are done only when HRV is within or above that range, and moderate aerobic work replaces them when HRV is below it.

Absolute HRV varies strongly between individuals by age, sex, fitness and genetics, so only within-person trends are meaningful. HRV markedly above baseline together with declining performance or persistent fatigue should raise suspicion of overreaching.

The review summarises evidence that HRV-guided training achieved similar or better gains with fewer high-intensity sessions, citing Vesterinen et al. (2016) in recreational runners and a trial in patients with coronary artery disease.

Consumer wearables estimate HRV optically from pulse waves, which can disagree with ECG-derived HRV, particularly in people with cardiometabolic disease. Accuracy is best at rest or during sleep, which is why most devices rely on overnight or morning recordings.
entries.relevance: The relevance for Došlap is limited. Its three-step model is a clear practical summary that matches the engine's approach, and its note on overnight optical measurement is relevant to Garmin data. However, its target population is clinical, and its suggestion that HRV-guided training may reduce injury risk is not supported by data in the review. For runner-facing cards, the primary sources it cites, Vesterinen et al. (2016) and Plews et al. (2014), should be used instead.
entries.limits: This is a narrative review without a systematic search or quality appraisal, and it focuses on patients. The runner data it reports are second-hand and should be checked against Vesterinen et al. (2016) once that paper is downloaded. Evidence strength for the card: very low for runners.
entries.strength: very low for runners.

entries.apa: Plews, D. J., Laursen, P. B., Kilding, A. E., & Buchheit, M. (2012). Heart rate variability in elite triathletes, is variation in variability the key to effective training? A case comparison. European Journal of Applied Physiology, 112(11), 3729–3741. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-012-2354-4

facts.Design: Case comparison with 77 days of daily morning HRV monitoring
facts.Participants: Two elite triathletes (a man aged 22 with VO₂max 72.5 and a woman aged 20 with VO₂max 68.2 ml/kg/min) training 23 ± 2 hours per week
facts.Event: The female athlete performed poorly in a key race, was diagnosed as non-functionally overreached (NFOR) and later developed shingles, whereas the male athlete served as the control
facts.Measures: Morning supine Ln rMSSD, its 7-day rolling average, the coefficient of variation (CV) of that average, resting heart rate, and daily ratings of sleep quality, muscle soreness and fatigue
facts.Main result: The 7-day rolling Ln rMSSD and its day-to-day variation declined toward NFOR, while both remained stable in the control athlete

findings: In the NFOR athlete, the 7-day rolling average of Ln rMSSD declined steadily towards the race, whereas it remained stable in the control athlete.

The day-to-day variation of HRV also fell progressively in the NFOR athlete (about −0.65% per week) but not in the control. The authors suggest that unusually stable HRV may be an early sign of NFOR, and that this marker can be used whether HRV rises or falls.

Single-day values were unreliable. In the control athlete, who was training well, 63.6% of single-day values fell outside the individual smallest worthwhile change, whereas after weekly averaging 18.2% fell above and 18.2% below it.
HRV showed a slightly stronger trend toward NFOR than resting heart rate, which also rose gradually.
The authors suggest that two consecutive weeks of unfavourable HRV trends may be more cause for concern than a single week.
entries.relevance: This case supports the engine's use of a 7-day rolling HRV and points to a secondary signal, unusually low day-to-day HRV variation, that the engine could monitor. It also supports requiring a sustained trend, for example two consecutive weeks, before HRV triggers a readiness warning, rather than reacting to one bad day or week. Because these ideas come from only two athletes, they should be treated as hypotheses rather than rules.
entries.limits: This is a descriptive comparison of two elite triathletes around a single event. The paper also reports some r² values as negative, which is not mathematically possible and presumably reflects the direction of the slope. Evidence strength for the card: very low, useful mainly as an illustration.
entries.strength: very low, useful mainly as an illustration.

entries.apa: Plews, D. J., Laursen, P. B., Stanley, J., Kilding, A. E., & Buchheit, M. (2013). Training adaptation and heart rate variability in elite endurance athletes: Opening the door to effective monitoring. Sports Medicine, 43(9), 773–781. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-013-0071-8

facts.Type: Current opinion article (narrative review with case data), one of the engine v3 references
facts.Evidence base: Literature on sedentary to elite endurance athletes, plus daily morning HRV data from Olympic and World Champion rowers
facts.Measurement: Morning HRV on waking, supine, analysed over the last 5 minutes of a 6-minute recording
facts.Main message: HRV monitoring is promising, but responses are individual and depend on training history, so a weekly or 7-day rolling Ln rMSSD compared with the individual's smallest worthwhile change is recommended

findings: In sedentary and recreationally trained people, endurance training typically increases both aerobic fitness and HRV. In one cited study, improvements in 10 km time were strongly correlated with increases in resting HRV (r = −0.73).

Very high training loads typically reduce HRV, which then rebounds during lighter training. After 3 weeks of overload, HRV fell by 22% in swimmers and by 38% in distance runners, and it rose again once training was reduced.

In elite and highly trained athletes the relationship between HRV and fitness or load is bell-shaped, and overtraining studies have reported increases, decreases and no change in HRV. HRV may also fall despite a lower resting heart rate, which the authors call HRV 'saturation'.
Single-day values can be misleading. In one cited study, changes in 10 km performance correlated very strongly with weekly averaged HRV (r = −0.76) but not with single-day values (r = −0.17).

The authors recommend using one index, Ln rMSSD, which has a much lower day-to-day error than spectral indices (coefficient of variation 12.3% versus 52.0%), assessed as a weekly or 7-day rolling average against the individual's smallest worthwhile change. In elite athletes, the ratio of Ln rMSSD to R–R interval can help distinguish saturation from fatigue.
entries.relevance: This is the core source for how the engine should treat HRV. It supports using one index, averaged over a week or a rolling 7 days, and comparing it with the runner's own normal range, which means a single low morning value should not on its own change the recommendation. The bell-shaped response in highly trained athletes also means that a rising HRV is not automatically good news, which matters for experienced Došlap users.
