Garmin records HRV overnight with a wrist sensor rather than as a supine morning recording, so the numerical values in this paper cannot be transferred one-to-one. This last caveat is my own and is not discussed by the authors.
entries.limits: This is an opinion article with case examples from a few elite rowers and no systematic search. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for the recommendation to average HRV over several days, which is supported by Plews et al. (2012, 2014), and low for the elite-specific interpretation.
entries.strength: moderate for the recommendation to average HRV over several days, which is supported by Plews et al. (2012, 2014), and low for the elite-specific interpretation

entries.apa: Plews, D. J., Laursen, P. B., Le Meur, Y., Hausswirth, C., Kilding, A. E., & Buchheit, M. (2014). Monitoring training with heart-rate variability: How much compliance is needed for valid assessment? International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 9(5), 783–790. https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2013-0455

facts.Design: Secondary analysis of two published data sets, in which 1 to 7 randomly selected days per week were averaged and compared
facts.Participants: 20 trained triathletes (13 functionally overreached, 7 controls) over 5 weeks, including 3 weeks of overload with 40% more load and a taper, and 10 recreational runners who responded to a 9-week training programme
facts.Measurement: Morning supine Ln rMSSD recorded with a chest-strap heart rate monitor
facts.Main result: At least 3 valid recordings per week were needed in trained triathletes and about 5 in recreational runners
facts.Version note: The downloaded PDF is the accepted manuscript from November 2013. The final version is 9(5), 783–790, and is the one to cite.

findings: In the triathletes, the standardised change in Ln rMSSD during overload stabilised once at least 3 days per week were averaged (0.20 with 1 day, 0.49 with 3 days and 0.43 with 7 days), and correlations with performance stabilised after 4 days.

Recreational runners had larger day-to-day variation in HRV (CV about 10% versus about 7% in the triathletes at baseline). Their positive adaptation to training was only reliably detected after averaging 5 days, and the correlation with 10 km performance had not stabilised even at 7 days.
The authors conclude that trained athletes need at least 3 valid recordings per week and less trained individuals probably around 5.

In the functionally overreached triathletes, HRV increased rather than decreased during overload, and after the taper HRV fell in some athletes and rose in others, even though all of them improved their performance. The authors stress that HRV responses are individual.
The authors also note that in an earlier study only 14 of 40 athletes collected enough morning recordings to be included, which shows that compliance is a real practical problem.
entries.relevance: This study gives the engine a concrete data-quality rule: HRV should only influence the recommendation once there are enough valid recordings, about 5 per week for recreational runners and at least 3 for well-trained runners. Garmin records HRV automatically overnight, so compliance may be higher than with manual morning recordings, but nights without valid data should still be counted. This application to Garmin is my own inference. The finding that HRV rose during functional overreaching also reinforces that the engine should not treat a higher HRV as always positive.
entries.limits: The analysis is based on two small data sets, only one performance test was available for the runners, and the recordings were manual morning measurements rather than overnight wearable data. Evidence strength for the card: low to moderate.
entries.strength: low to moderate.

entries.apa: Schaffarczyk, M., & Sperlich, B. (2026). Heart rate variability–guided endurance training: Evaluating strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats for load prescription and adjustment. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, 8, Article 1858271. https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2026.1858271

facts.Type: Perspective article using a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT) framework, not a systematic review
facts.Evidence base: Mainly the two 2021 meta-analyses of HRV-guided training (Düking et al. and Manresa-Rocamora et al., each with 8 controlled studies), plus methodological and wearable literature
facts.Main message: The main limitation of HRV-guided training is no longer the availability of data but the lack of transparent, physiologically grounded rules for turning HRV into training decisions
facts.Note: Published on 27 August 2026 and not on the original download list. Its metadata were verified through Crossref.

findings: According to the two 2021 meta-analyses, HRV-guided training gave no significant advantage for VO₂max or endurance performance (pooled effects trivial to small), whereas effects on submaximal and threshold-related outcomes and on vagal HRV were more favourable. Individual studies also reported fewer negative responders.

Current practice has moved from single-day values to 7-day rolling averages interpreted against individual normal ranges, with Ln rMSSD as the preferred index. Resting heart rate, the Ln rMSSD to R–R ratio and the day-to-day variation of Ln rMSSD are proposed as complementary markers.

HRV is described as a global and non-specific marker that also responds to illness, alcohol, menstrual cycle phase, sleep, hydration and environmental factors. Higher HRV is not inherently favourable, and HRV says little about muscle recovery, so it should not be the sole basis for training decisions.

Wrist and ring wearables measure pulse rate variability optically, which is not fully interchangeable with ECG-derived HRV, although it may give acceptable estimates for standardised monitoring at rest.

Trials have used many different decision rules, such as the individual mean ± 0.5 SD or a rolling 4-week average ± 0.5 SD, and there is no consensus on which is best. Commercial readiness scores are criticised as opaque and insufficiently validated, and the authors call for frameworks that state which signals are used, how they are weighted and how conflicting signals are resolved.
entries.relevance: This paper is highly relevant, because it describes almost exactly the design problem Došlap is addressing. It supports the principle in the Phase 2 plan that the engine is the transparent source of truth and the AI only explains its recommendation, and it argues against relying on proprietary readiness scores. It also lists concrete decision rules used in trials, such as the mean ± 0.5 SD, which the engine could adopt while stating that none is established as best. For any evidence card, the meta-analytic results it summarises should be cited from the primary meta-analysis by Manresa-Rocamora et al. (2021), which is summarised in this section.
entries.limits: This is a perspective paper by two authors without a systematic search, and its evidence summaries are second-hand. Evidence strength for the card: useful as a framework and for the limits field, not as the source of an effect claim.
entries.strength: useful as a framework and for the limits field, not as the source of an effect claim.

entries.apa: Casado, A., González-Mohíno, F., González-Ravé, J. M., & Foster, C. (2022). Training periodization, methods, intensity distribution, and volume in highly trained and elite distance runners: A systematic review. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 17(6), 820–833. https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.2021-0435

facts.Design: Systematic review of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science
facts.Studies included: 10 studies of highly trained and elite middle- and long-distance runners, including 4 case studies and only 4 experimental studies
facts.Quality appraisal: 15-item checklist, with a mean score of 12.5 out of 15
facts.Main result: Elite distance runners typically follow a pyramidal intensity distribution that shifts toward a polarised distribution in the competitive period
facts.Version note: The downloaded PDF is the ahead-of-print version from April 2022. The final version is 17(6), 820–833.

findings: Three intensity zones are defined: zone 1 at or below the first threshold, zone 2 between the first and second thresholds, and zone 3 above the second threshold. In a pyramidal model about 80% of volume is in zone 1 and the remainder decreases from zone 2 to zone 3, whereas in a polarised model most of the remaining 20% is spent in zone 3.

Elite runners usually trained pyramidally during preparatory periods and became more polarised during the competitive period. Marathon runners trained more pyramidally and 1500 m runners more polarised.
A 'hard day–easy day' pattern was routinely observed, with at least three easy days per week and a long run that typically drifted from zone 1 into zone 2.
Higher performance was associated with higher training volume, typically 110 to 195 km per week, and with at least one session near the second threshold and one session in zone 3 each week.

The authors acknowledge that most studies were observational or case studies, so they cannot show whether a pyramidal or a polarised approach is superior, and their conclusions assume that elite runners optimise their own training.
entries.relevance: This review shows that the rigid '80/20 polarised' message is too simple even for elite runners, many of whom use a pyramidal distribution with meaningful threshold work. For the engine, the robust common principles are a large share of easy running and a hard-day, easy-day structure, rather than a fixed polarised template. Its volume figures, above 100 km per week, describe elite athletes and should not be used as targets for Došlap users.
entries.limits: Only 10 studies were available, several were case studies, and the comparison between event distances was made within a single coach's training group. Evidence strength for the card: low to moderate, since it describes elite practice rather than testing it.
entries.strength: low to moderate, since it describes elite practice rather than testing it.

entries.apa: Seiler, S. (2010). What is best practice for training intensity and duration distribution in endurance athletes? International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 5(3), 276–291. https://doi.org/10.1123/ijspp.5.3.276

facts.Type: Brief narrative review, single author, one of the engine v3 references
facts.Evidence base: Descriptive studies of national and international endurance athletes training 10 to 13 times per week, plus studies that intensified the training of well-trained athletes
facts.Main message: Successful endurance athletes do about 80% of sessions at low intensity (below about 2 mmol/L blood lactate) and about 20% at threshold or high intensity, and adding more high-intensity training for already well-trained athletes shows no convincing long-term benefit

findings: Across descriptive studies, about 80% of training sessions are performed at low intensity and about 20% involve threshold or high-intensity work, which for an athlete training 10 to 14 times per week means two to three hard sessions.

Adding two interval sessions per week for 4 to 8 weeks improved performance by 2% to 4% in well-trained athletes who had been doing only basic endurance training. However, further increases in interval frequency brought no additional benefit and tended to cause signs of overreaching.
In a cited study of Spanish distance runners with matched total load, the group that did more low-intensity training (81% versus 67% of time) improved race time more (−157 versus −121.5 s).

Heart-rate time-in-zone analysis overestimates easy time and underestimates hard time, because heart rate lags during intervals. Classifying each session by its main goal (the 'session goal approach') matches athletes' perceived effort better.

HRV recovers quickly after up to 120 minutes at about 60% of VO₂max, but recovery is markedly delayed when intensity exceeds about 3 mmol/L lactate, which may help explain why most training is kept easy.
entries.relevance: This is the main source for how the engine balances easy and hard sessions. It supports a default in which most weekly sessions are easy and only two or three are hard, and it explains why recommending an easy session is often the evidence-based choice. The point about time-in-zone also matters for how Došlap labels sessions, since an interval session should count as a hard session even if heart rate spent most of the time in the easy zone. The evidence describes mainly elite athletes who train up to twice a day, so applying it to recreational runners who train three to five times a week is an assumption. This caveat is my own.
entries.limits: This is a narrative review by a leading proponent of the polarised model, based mainly on descriptive data from elite athletes and few controlled trials. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for the descriptive 80/20 pattern in elite athletes, low for its direct application to recreational runners.
entries.strength: moderate for the descriptive 80/20 pattern in elite athletes, low for its direct application to recreational runners.

entries.apa: Stöggl, T., & Sperlich, B. (2014). Polarized training has greater impact on key endurance variables than threshold, high intensity, or high volume training. Frontiers in Physiology, 5, Article 33. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2014.00033

facts.Design: Randomised trial, 9 weeks
facts.Participants: 48 well-trained endurance athletes (21 runners, 15 cyclists, 8 cross-country skiers, 4 triathletes), mean age 31, VO₂peak 62.6 ml/kg/min, training 10 to 20 hours per week
facts.Groups: High-volume low-intensity (HVT), threshold (THR), high-intensity interval (HIIT) and polarised training (POL, about 68% low, 6% threshold and 26% high intensity)
facts.Outcomes: VO₂peak, time to exhaustion, peak velocity or power, velocity or power at 4 mmol/L lactate, work economy and body mass
facts.Main result: POL produced the largest improvements in most variables, whereas HVT and THR produced no further improvements

findings: POL increased VO₂peak by 11.7% (+6.8 ml/kg/min), time to exhaustion by 17.4% and peak velocity or power by 5.1%, which were the largest gains of the four groups.
Velocity or power at 4 mmol/L improved after POL (+8.1%) and HIIT (+5.6%), while work economy did not differ between groups.
HIIT reduced body mass by 3.7% (about 3 kg). The authors caution that this may be undesirable over longer periods and that 9 weeks of HIIT should be applied with care.
HVT and THR produced no further improvements in endurance variables, apart from a slight improvement in work economy with THR.
Before the study, none of the athletes had done HIIT regularly, and all had trained mainly with high volume and at most two threshold sessions per week.
entries.relevance: This trial supports including a small number of genuinely hard sessions alongside mostly easy running, rather than accumulating a lot of moderate threshold running. For the engine, it justifies keeping easy days easy and hard days hard. However, the polarised group spent 26% of its training at high intensity, more than the roughly 20% seen in descriptive data, and the athletes were new to HIIT, so part of the effect may reflect the novelty of the stimulus. This interpretation is my own and is not stated by the authors.
entries.limits: The groups were small (about 12 athletes each), the study lasted only 9 weeks, the outcomes were laboratory tests rather than races, and several sports were mixed. The authors themselves describe the 11.7% gain in VO₂peak as large for well-trained athletes and call for longer studies. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for short-term physiological gains, low for long-term race performance in recreational runners.
entries.strength: moderate for short-term physiological gains, low for long-term race performance in recreational runners.

entries.apa: Treff, G., Alimoradinasrabadi, B., Nusser, V., Steinacker, J., Köhler, K., & Winkert, K. (2026). Not all low-intensity rowing is the same: Self-paced intensity exceeds formula-based heart-rate–guided low-intensity on-water rowing in elite rowers [Conference abstract]. Current Issues in Sport Science, 11(5), 037. https://doi.org/10.36950/2026.5ciss037

facts.Type: Conference abstract published in Current Issues in Sport Science (September 2026), not a full peer-reviewed article
facts.Design: Four on-water trials per rower (two self-paced and two heart-rate-guided), each with six 15-minute steps at 'very low', 'low' and 'moderate' intensity, with heart-rate targets of 60–72%, 72–79% and 79–82% of maximum
facts.Main result: Self-paced rowing was consistently harder and more variable than heart-rate-guided rowing, and even with guidance the 'low' zone was not below the first lactate threshold
facts.Note: Not on the original download list. The uploaded file contains only Figure 1, so this summary is based on the abstract in the Crossref record.

findings: Across all zones, self-paced rowing produced significantly higher %HRmax and %VO₂max than heart-rate-guided rowing (p < .01), and variability between rowers was consistently smaller with heart-rate guidance.
Self-paced 'low' intensity did not differ from heart-rate-guided 'moderate' intensity, which means that rowers relying on their own feel drifted into the moderate zone during intended easy work.

Blood lactate did not distinguish 'very low' from 'low' (about 1.1 to 1.2 mmol/L), and perceived exertion did not differ between self-paced and guided trials, so the athletes did not perceive that they were going harder.

Even with heart-rate guidance, the 'low' zone was not significantly below the first lactate threshold, so fixed percentage-of-maximum targets did not reliably keep easy training easy. The authors recommend anchoring easy-training targets to each athlete's individual first threshold.
entries.relevance: This abstract is directly relevant to Došlap's daily session commentary. It suggests that athletes asked to train easy without external feedback tend to go too hard without noticing, which justifies giving the runner a concrete heart-rate range for easy sessions. It also warns that generic percentage-of-maximum zones may be set too high, which supports individual zones based on a threshold estimate where the engine has one. Transfer from elite rowers to recreational runners is an assumption, and this caveat is my own.
entries.limits: This is a short conference abstract with 15 elite rowers, and I could review only the abstract and one figure. Evidence strength for the card: very low, useful only as a supporting illustration. The abstract cites a network meta-analysis by Rosenblat et al. (2025), which may be worth downloading for this section.
entries.strength: very low, useful only as a supporting illustration. The abstract cites a network meta-analysis by Rosenblat et al

entries.apa: Looney, D. P., Hoogkamer, W., & Kram, R. (2026). Metabolic energy expenditure during level, uphill, and downhill running. European Journal of Applied Physiology, 126(3), 1621–1633. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00421-025-05999-5

facts.Type: Original study that pools metabolic data to develop and validate prediction equations
facts.Data: An original data set of 62 runners, individual data from 26 studies (424 participants) and group means from 12 studies (187 participants)
facts.Grades covered: From −45% to +82%, the widest range of any running equation to date
facts.Equations: A new graded term for the Running Energy Expenditure
facts.compared: Estimation (RE3) model and an updated Hoogkamer-Taboga-Kram (HTK) equation, compared with the ACSM equation and Minetti et al. (2002)
facts.Main result: RE3 and HTK were the most accurate on level and uphill ground, RE3 was marginally better than Minetti et al. downhill, and the ACSM equation was clearly the least accurate
facts.Note: Published online in October 2025 (issue dated March 2026) and not on the original download list

findings: On level ground, RE3 (root-mean-square deviation 1.27 W/kg), HTK (1.30) and Minetti et al. (1.44) estimated metabolic rate well, whereas the widely used ACSM equation was much less accurate (1.82).
Uphill, HTK (1.45) and RE3 (1.41) were clearly more accurate than ACSM (2.17) and Minetti et al. (2.18). Downhill, RE3 was marginally better than Minetti et al. (1.45 versus 1.57).
Existing equations can disagree strongly, and in one worked example at slow speed the ACSM and Minetti estimates differed almost two-fold (17.0 versus 27.9 W/kg).

The equations estimate cost for an average runner. Running economy can differ by up to 30% between trained runners with a similar VO₂max, economy on the level does not always carry over to steep slopes, and downhill cost is harder to model because VO₂ can rise by up to 10% over 40 to 45 minutes of downhill running.
The authors provide a free web calculator for the updated RE3 model.
entries.relevance: This study gives the engine a validated way to convert distance, speed and gradient into an estimate of metabolic cost, which could make the load of hilly and trail runs comparable with flat runs, for example as a grade-adjusted load. It also suggests avoiding the ACSM equation for graded running. Because the estimates describe an average runner, they are best used to adjust load rather than to predict an individual's effort, for which heart rate remains the better signal. Metabolic cost also does not capture mechanical load, so a descent can be energetically cheap but mechanically demanding, as Vernillo et al. (2017) describe. Combining the two in this way is my own suggestion.
entries.limits: The equations estimate metabolic rate, not injury risk or tissue load, and they are based mainly on treadmill data for an average runner. Downhill modelling remains limited, especially on grades steeper than about −15%. Evidence strength for the card: moderate to high for estimating average energy cost, not applicable to injury claims.
entries.strength: moderate to high for estimating average energy cost, not applicable to injury claims.

entries.apa: Martínez-Gramage, J., Pardo Albiach, J., Nacher Moltó, I., Amer-Cuenca, J. J., Huesa Moreno, V., Varangot-Reille, C., Barea Tarín, L., Perpiñá Martínez, S., & Segura-Ortí, E. (2020). Does running gait retraining decrease running injury incidence in young triathletes? [Poster presentation]. Universidad Cardenal Herrera-CEU, Valencia, Spain.

facts.Type: Conference poster from 2020, not a peer-reviewed article and without a DOI. The conference name is not stated on the poster.
facts.Participants: 19 young triathletes aged 11 to 18 (10 boys, 9 girls) from the Valencian Community triathlon specialisation programme
facts.Design: 7-month gait retraining programme with assessments at the start and end, and no control group
facts.Measures: Self-reported injuries, and kinematics, surface EMG and inertial sensor data at 90% of maximal aerobic speed, analysed with a random forest classification
facts.Main result: Fewer injuries after the programme, about 8 in 2018 versus about 2 in 2019 according to the poster's bar chart
facts.Note: Not on the original download list. The same group published a related full paper: Martínez-Gramage et al. (2020), Sensors, 20(21), 6388, https://doi.org/10.3390/s20216388 (verified through Crossref, content not yet reviewed).

findings: The number of injuries fell from about 8 in 2018 to about 2 in 2019, as read from the poster's bar chart. No statistical test is reported for this change.
After the programme, stride rate increased from 174.4 to 181.4 steps per minute (p ≤ .05) and run cycle time decreased from 0.69 to 0.66 s, while running speed did not change significantly.

The random forest analysis identified greater contralateral pelvic drop and lower gluteus medius activation as the variables most related to injury. After retraining, the athletes showed less pelvic drop, more gluteus medius activation, more trunk extension and knee flexion, and less ankle dorsiflexion at initial contact.
entries.relevance: This poster offers weak preliminary support for gait retraining and for pelvic drop as a target that a physiotherapist on Došlap might address. It should not support any engine rule or runner-facing claim that retraining prevents injury, since it is a before-and-after comparison in adolescents without a control group, and a year-to-year drop in injuries could reflect many other factors. If gait retraining becomes a card topic, Barton et al. (2016) on the download list is the stronger source, and the full Sensors paper should be reviewed.
entries.limits: This is a poster with 19 adolescents, no control group, self-reported injuries, and injury counts that can only be read from a chart. Evidence strength for the card: very low.
entries.strength: very low.

entries.apa: Moore, I. S. (2016). Is there an economical running technique? A review of modifiable biomechanical factors affecting running economy. Sports Medicine, 46(6), 793–807. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-016-0474-4

facts.Type: Narrative review, single author, open access
facts.Scope: Intrinsic and extrinsic modifiable biomechanical factors affecting running economy, and whether training or retraining changes them
facts.Main message: Several factors are associated with better economy, especially during push-off, but recommending a general economical running technique should be approached with caution

findings: Runners tend to self-optimise their stride. In trained runners the most economical stride frequency is on average only about 3% faster than their preferred one, and shortening stride length by 3% did not worsen economy, whereas deviations above 6% did. In novice runners the gap between preferred and optimal stride frequency was larger, at about 8%.
Foot strike pattern had a negligible effect on economy. However, forcing habitual rearfoot strikers to land on the forefoot worsened economy at slow and medium speeds.

Factors linked with better economy included lower vertical oscillation, greater leg stiffness, less leg extension at toe-off, maintaining arm swing, and running barefoot or in lightweight shoes, whereas ground contact time, trunk lean and orthotics showed inconsistent relationships.

Retraining toward global techniques such as Pose or Chi running did not improve economy and sometimes worsened it. By contrast, one study showed that gait retraining aimed at reducing impact loading lowered tibial acceleration without changing economy.
Novice runners improved their economy over 10 weeks of normal running through self-optimisation, whereas trained runners showed little further change.
entries.relevance: This review supports cautious messaging about running technique. The engine should not push runners toward a particular foot strike or global technique for the sake of efficiency, and changes in watch metrics such as cadence or vertical oscillation are better treated as trends to monitor than as faults to correct. The data on the 3% range also suggest that a small increase in cadence, which a physiotherapist might prescribe for injury reasons, is unlikely to cost economy. This last point is my own inference.
entries.limits: This is a narrative review of largely cross-sectional and short-term studies, mostly in trained runners on treadmills, and it concerns running economy rather than injury. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for the claim that no universal economical technique exists, low for any specific metric threshold.
entries.strength: moderate for the claim that no universal economical technique exists, low for any specific metric threshold.

entries.apa: Vernillo, G., Giandolini, M., Edwards, W. B., Morin, J.-B., Samozino, P., Horvais, N., & Millet, G. Y. (2017). Biomechanics and physiology of uphill and downhill running. Sports Medicine, 47(4), 615–629. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-016-0605-y

facts.Type: Narrative review
facts.Scope: Biomechanical, neuromuscular and physiological adaptations to uphill and downhill running compared with level running
facts.Main message: Slope changes stride pattern, foot strike, ground reaction forces, muscle work and energy cost, with implications for injury prevention and pacing

findings: Uphill running is characterised by a higher step frequency, a shorter aerial phase and a shift toward mid- or forefoot striking, whereas downhill running shows a longer aerial phase, a lower step frequency and more rearfoot striking.

Downhill running increases impact forces and braking. In cited studies, impact peaks were higher at −7% than on level or uphill ground, and at −15.8% the braking impulse was 108% greater than on level ground. Tibial shock increased by about 30% on a −8.7% slope in one study, although shock attenuation varied considerably between individuals.

Uphill running requires more positive muscle work, particularly at the hip, and overall joint work was about 28% higher uphill than downhill. The knee performed most of the negative, braking work in both directions.

Energy cost rises linearly with uphill slope and falls with downhill slope until a minimum at about −20%, after which it rises again. Natural changes in pace on hills are not enough to keep effort constant, since in one study VO₂ reached 100% of the ventilatory threshold uphill, compared with 89% on the level and 79% downhill.

Two hours of running at a 10% incline depleted more muscle glycogen than level running at the same relative intensity, and perceived exertion tended to be higher downhill at the same blood lactate level.
entries.relevance: This review directly supports the engine's terrain findings. First, a run with a lot of descent loads tissues, especially around the knee and shin, more than its distance and pace suggest, even though heart rate may be lower. Second, uphill running raises metabolic demand beyond what pace alone shows. Load based on pace should therefore be adjusted for gradient, and a trail run with substantial descent could be flagged as mechanically demanding. The specific numbers come from small laboratory studies on treadmills or short road sections.
entries.limits: This is a narrative review of mostly small laboratory studies on moderate slopes, and it reports no direct injury outcomes, so the injury implications are the authors' inference. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for the biomechanical and energy-cost effects of slope, low for injury risk.
entries.strength: moderate for the biomechanical and energy-cost effects of slope, low for injury risk.

entries.apa: Périard, J. D., Racinais, S., & Sawka, M. N. (2015). Adaptations and mechanisms of human heat acclimation: Applications for competitive athletes and sports. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, 25(Suppl. 1), 20–38. https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.12408

facts.Type: Narrative review from the same research group and journal supplement as the heat consensus
facts.Scope: Physiological adaptations to heat acclimation and their application to competitive athletes
facts.Main message: Heat acclimation improves sweating, skin blood flow, plasma volume and cardiovascular stability, lowers body temperature and heart rate, and improves aerobic performance in the heat

findings: About 75% to 80% of adaptations occur in the first 4 to 7 days. The reduction in exercise heart rate develops fastest over 4 to 5 days and is virtually complete after 7 days, while thermoregulatory benefits are generally complete after 10 to 14 days.

On the first days of exercise in the heat, heart rate is much higher and stroke volume lower than in temperate conditions at the same work rate. Plasma volume usually expands by about 4% to 15% within 3 to 4 days of repeated heat exposure.
In a cited field study, cycling time-trial power in the heat (about 37 °C) was markedly reduced at first, partly recovered after 1 week of acclimatisation and almost fully restored after 2 weeks.

Heart-rate benefits are lost faster than thermoregulatory ones. Estimates of decay vary widely, from losses of nearly 100% for heart rate after 3 weeks in sedentary people to minimal decay over 12 to 26 days in people who stay physically active, which suggests that fitness and regular exercise help retain the adaptations.

Improved sweating is described as the most critical adaptation. Adaptations to dry and humid heat transfer partly, but acclimatising in conditions similar to those of competition gives the most specific adaptation.
entries.relevance: This review explains why heart rate at a given pace rises on the first hot days and falls again over the following week. For the engine, a hot-weather rise in heart rate should therefore not be read as a loss of fitness or poor readiness, and the heat adjustment could be relaxed gradually over about one to two weeks of repeated hot runs. Using this time course in the engine is my own application.
entries.limits: This is a narrative review in which much of the evidence comes from laboratory, military and older studies, often in men, and the rate at which adaptations decay remains disputed. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for the time course of adaptation, low for precise decay estimates.
entries.strength: moderate for the time course of adaptation, low for precise decay estimates.

entries.apa: Racinais, S., Alonso, J. M., Coutts, A. J., Flouris, A. D., Girard, O., González-Alonso, J., Hausswirth, C., Jay, O., Lee, J. K. W., Mitchell, N., Nassis, G. P., Nybo, L., Pluim, B. M., Roelands, B., Sawka, M. N., Wingo, J., & Périard, J. D. (2015). Consensus recommendations on training and competing in the heat. Sports Medicine, 45(7), 925–938. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0343-6

facts.Type: Expert consensus statement by 17 authors, published simultaneously in Sports Medicine, the British Journal of Sports Medicine (49(18), 1164–1173) and the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports (25(S1), 6–19)
facts.Scope: Heat acclimatisation, hydration, cooling strategies and recommendations for event organisers
facts.Main message: Heat acclimatisation over 1 to 2 weeks is the most important intervention, combined with starting exercise well hydrated and limiting dehydration
facts.Note: You uploaded both the Sports Medicine and the BJSM versions. They carry the same content, so they are summarised here as one source, and only one version should be cited.

findings: Most adaptations, including lower heart rate, lower skin and core temperature and a higher sweat rate, develop within the first week of heat exposure. However, 6 to 10 days are needed for near-complete cardiovascular and sweating adaptations and about 2 weeks to optimise performance, and highly trained athletes adapt up to twice as fast as untrained people.

Acclimatisation sessions should last at least 60 minutes per day and raise core and skin temperature enough to cause heavy sweating. Training in temperate conditions gives only partial acclimatisation, and most benefits are retained for 2 to 4 weeks after heat exposure ends, with faster re-acclimatisation afterwards.

Dehydration beyond about 2% of body mass is reported to impair aerobic performance in warm to hot conditions, although some studies of trained cyclists found no impairment up to 4%. The consensus advises limiting losses to about 2% to 3% when sweat rates are high, while warning recreational athletes not to overdrink because of the risk of hyponatraemia, particularly in events longer than 4 hours, in women and in people with a low body mass index.

Sweat rates of 1.0 to 1.5 litres per hour are common in hot conditions and can exceed 2.5 litres per hour. For exercise longer than an hour, fluids with 0.5 to 0.7 g of sodium per litre and 30 to 60 g of carbohydrate per hour are recommended.

The Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) index is widely used to adjust or cancel events, but it can underestimate heat stress in high humidity or still air and ignores metabolic heat and clothing. The risk of heat illness appears higher early in summer and during sudden hot spells, when people are not yet acclimatised.
entries.relevance: This consensus provides the evidence base for the engine's weather adjustments. It supports being more cautious on the first hot days of the season and during sudden hot spells, and it suggests that this extra caution can ease only after about one to two weeks of repeated runs in the heat. It also supports combining temperature with humidity rather than using temperature alone. The hydration and sodium figures are nutritional guidance, so the AI texts should mention them only in general terms and should not prescribe fluid volumes, given the risk of overdrinking in recreational runners. Linking the acclimatisation timeline to how quickly the engine relaxes its heat adjustment is my own suggestion.
entries.limits: This is an expert consensus aimed mainly at elite athletes competing in the heat and supported largely by laboratory studies, and parts of the hydration and cooling advice remain debated. Evidence strength for the card: moderate to high for the acclimatisation timeline, moderate for the hydration thresholds.
entries.strength: moderate to high for the acclimatisation timeline, moderate for the hydration thresholds.

entries.apa: Gao, B., Dwivedi, S., Milewski, M. D., & Cruz, A. I., Jr. (2019). Chronic lack of sleep is associated with increased sports injury in adolescents: A systematic review and meta-analysis [Conference abstract]. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine, 7(3_suppl), Article 2325967119S00132. https://doi.org/10.1177/2325967119S00132

facts.Type: Conference abstract from the 6th Annual Meeting of the Pediatric Research in Sports Medicine Society (PRiSM), published in a journal supplement
facts.Design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of PubMed and Embase, 1997 to 2017
facts.Studies included: 7 of 907 records (6 cohort studies and 1 case series) in adolescents under 19
facts.Quality appraisal: Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, with five cohort studies rated at moderate risk of bias and one at low risk
facts.Main result: Chronically poor sleepers were more likely to be injured (OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.37), pooled from three studies
facts.Note: This is not the original cohort study by Milewski et al. (2014) on the download list, although Milewski is a co-author. The original study is still needed.

findings: Five of the seven studies found that adolescents who chronically slept poorly were significantly more likely to sustain a sports or musculoskeletal injury.
In the meta-analysis of three studies, chronically poor sleepers had higher odds of injury than good sleepers (OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.37, p = .03).
Evidence on short-term poor sleep was inconclusive, since one study found a positive association and another found none.
All studies relied on self-reported sleep hours, which was the most consistent source of bias.
The authors conclude that adolescents who chronically sleep less than 8 hours per night or wake frequently are more likely to be injured.
entries.relevance: This abstract offers pooled support for a link between chronic short sleep and injury, but only in adolescents, so its relevance to Došlap's adult runners is indirect. It supports treating a chronic sleep deficit, rather than a single bad night, as the relevant signal, which is consistent with Halson (2014b). The injury figure of 1.7 cited by Kaczmarek et al. (2025) differs from the pooled estimate of 1.58 here, which shows why figures should be taken from primary sources.
entries.limits: This is a conference abstract in which only three observational studies were pooled, all in adolescents and all based on self-reported sleep. Evidence strength for the card: low, and very low for adults.
entries.strength: low, and very low for adults.

entries.apa: Halson, S. L. (2014b). Sleep in elite athletes and nutritional interventions to enhance sleep. Sports Medicine, 44(Suppl. 1), 13–23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-014-0147-0

facts.Type: Narrative review, single author (Australian Institute of Sport), open access
facts.Scope: Sleep in elite athletes, effects of sleep deprivation and extension on performance, and nutritional interventions that may improve sleep
facts.Main message: Sleep loss can impair performance, particularly in submaximal, prolonged exercise, athletes may sleep less and worse than recommended, and nutritional interventions are promising but poorly supported
facts.Citation note: Because Halson also has another 2014 paper in Section B, the two should be cited as 2014a (monitoring training load) and 2014b (this paper), ordered by title in the reference list.

findings: Restricting sleep to less than 6 hours per night for 4 or more consecutive nights has been shown to impair cognition, mood, glucose metabolism, appetite regulation and immune function.

In one actigraphy study, elite athletes spent longer in bed than non-athletes (8 h 36 min versus 8 h 07 min) but took longer to fall asleep (18.2 versus 5.0 min) and had lower sleep efficiency (80.6% versus 88.7%), so their actual sleep time was similar (6 h 55 min versus 7 h 11 min).
Of 632 German athletes, 66% reported sleeping worse than normal at least once before an important competition, mostly because of difficulty falling asleep.

The effects of sleep loss are task-specific. After a night without sleep, men covered less distance in a 30-minute self-paced treadmill run (6,037 versus 6,224 m), and with partial sleep loss, submaximal and prolonged tasks appeared more affected than maximal efforts, particularly after the first two nights.

Proposed nutritional strategies, such as high-glycaemic carbohydrate more than 1 hour before bed, tryptophan, melatonin-rich foods and valerian, rest on limited and partly contradictory evidence, and the author warns about supplement contamination.
entries.relevance: This review supports including sleep in the engine's readiness assessment. Because the evidence points to cumulative effects on prolonged submaximal work, several consecutive short nights may matter more for an endurance session than a single bad night. This emphasis on consecutive nights is my own inference for the engine. The nutritional and supplement suggestions should not appear in Došlap texts, since melatonin and herbal supplements come close to the medication advice that the validator excludes.
entries.limits: This is a narrative review of mostly small laboratory studies, largely in men and often using more extreme sleep loss than athletes normally experience, and the nutritional evidence is weak. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for the effect of sleep loss on prolonged exercise, low for nutritional interventions.
entries.strength: moderate for the effect of sleep loss on prolonged exercise, low for nutritional interventions.

entries.apa: Kaczmarek, F., Bartkowiak-Wieczorek, J., Matecka, M., Jenczylik, K., Brzezińska, K., Gajniak, P., Marchwiak, S., Kaczmarek, K., Nowak, M., Kmiecik, M., Stężycka, J., Krupa, K. K., & Mądry, E. (2025). Sleep and athletic performance: A multidimensional review of physiological and molecular mechanisms. Journal of Clinical Medicine, 14(21), Article 7606. https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm14217606

facts.Type: Narrative review written largely by a student scientific society at Poznan University of Medical Sciences
facts.Method: Stepwise searches of PubMed/Medline and Cochrane, with about 7,700 records and 178 articles evaluated, and no formal quality appraisal of the included studies reported
facts.Scope: Sleep physiology, effects of sleep loss on performance and recovery, hormonal and molecular mechanisms, sleep assessment, travel, diet, supplements and treatment of sleep disorders
facts.Note: Not on the original download list

findings: Sleep restriction is described as impairing both submaximal and maximal performance, with higher heart rate, ventilation and lactate during exercise, earlier fatigue and reduced VO₂max, as well as impaired muscle strength and glycogen resynthesis.
Insufficient sleep is linked to hormonal changes that favour breakdown over repair, including higher cortisol and lower testosterone and growth hormone.

The review states that in young athletes, sleeping 8 hours or less is associated with a 1.7 times higher injury risk. This figure most likely originates from Milewski et al. (2014) on the download list, which should be checked as the primary source. This attribution is my own inference.

Endurance athletes are described as having a higher sleep need. Sleep extension and naps of 20 to 90 minutes are presented as useful, alongside sleep hygiene measures such as limiting evening caffeine and screen use.
The authors acknowledge that treating athletes as one homogeneous group ignores differences between sports, and that the selection of factors covered was selective.
entries.relevance: This review offers a broad background on why sleep matters for recovery, and it supports the engine including sleep in its readiness assessment. However, its claims are general, often second-hand and not specific to runners, so it should not be the source of any specific threshold on an evidence card. The primary studies and the 2021 expert consensus by Walsh et al. on the download list are better sources for runner-facing claims.
entries.limits: This is a broad narrative review without formal appraisal of study quality, it generalises across all sports, and most of its specific figures are cited from other reviews. Evidence strength for the card: low.
entries.strength: low.

entries.apa: Pyzik, A., Polakowska, A., Dziegciarczyk, A., Sobczak, W. L., Borkowska, K., Pielusiński, K. T., Swoboda, K., & Olejnik, M. (2026). Restoring the athlete: The role of sleep in athletic performance and recovery. Quality in Sport, 52, Article 69361. https://doi.org/10.12775/QS.2026.52.69361

facts.Type: Narrative review assessed against the SANRA criteria for narrative reviews
facts.Method: PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science searched for 2015 to 2025
facts.Scope: Sleep assessment in athletes and strategies to improve sleep, including sleep hygiene, sleep extension, napping, mindfulness, caffeine and travel
facts.Journal: Quality in Sport, whose assigned scientific disciplines are economics and management rather than sport or medical science
facts.Note: Not on the original download list. The paper states that it was accepted two months after its publication date, and Crossref lists the article number as 69360 while the PDF shows 69361.

findings: Actigraphy agrees acceptably with polysomnography for total sleep time and sleep efficiency at the group level, but it can misclassify quiet wakefulness as sleep and says little about sleep stages, so it is best used to monitor trends.

Elite athletes frequently report sleeping less than 7 hours with a sleep efficiency below 85%, especially during intensified training, competition and travel. Early-morning sessions tend to shorten sleep more than late-evening ones.
Individualised sleep hygiene education improved objective sleep efficiency and shortened the time to fall asleep in professional female footballers.
Naps of 30 to 60 minutes are reported to improve cognitive and physical performance and to reduce fatigue, and early-afternoon naps are less likely to disturb night sleep.
The review also mentions melatonin doses for jet lag. This is medication advice that Došlap's texts must not give.
entries.relevance: The point that watch-based sleep tracking is suited to trends rather than precise sleep stages supports how the engine should use Garmin sleep data, namely as a multi-night trend combined with the runner's own sleep rating. Beyond that, the review adds little for Došlap, and its weak publication context means it should not be cited on an evidence card.
entries.limits: This is a short narrative review in a journal outside sport and medical science, with inconsistencies in its publication dates and article number. Evidence strength for the card: very low.
entries.strength: very low.

entries.apa: Watson, N. F., Badr, M. S., Belenky, G., Bliwise, D. L., Buxton, O. M., Buysse, D., Dinges, D. F., Gangwisch, J., Grandner, M. A., Kushida, C., Malhotra, R. K., Martin, J. L., Patel, S. R., Quan, S. F., & Tasali, E. (2015). Recommended amount of sleep for a healthy adult: A joint consensus statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 11(6), 591–592. https://doi.org/10.5664/jcsm.4758

facts.Type: Joint consensus statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society, developed by a 15-member expert panel using a modified RAND Appropriateness Method
facts.Evidence base: 5,314 articles reviewed across nine health categories, including human performance
facts.Main: Adults should sleep 7 or more hours per night on a
facts.Version note: The same statement was published in SLEEP, 38(6), 843–844 (the DOI on the download list). Only one version should be cited.

findings: Adults should sleep 7 or more hours per night on a regular basis to promote optimal health.

Regularly sleeping less than 7 hours is associated with weight gain and obesity, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, stroke, depression and a higher risk of death, as well as with impaired immune function, increased pain, impaired performance, more errors and a greater risk of accidents.

Sleeping more than 9 hours per night may be appropriate for young adults, people recovering from sleep debt and people who are ill, while for others it is uncertain whether it carries any health risk.

Healthy sleep requires not only adequate duration but also good quality, appropriate timing and regularity, and the absence of sleep disorders, and individual sleep need varies with genetic, behavioural, medical and environmental factors.
People who are concerned that they sleep too little or too much should consult a healthcare provider.
entries.relevance: This statement provides the authoritative general threshold that the engine can use, namely that repeated nights under 7 hours lower readiness. It does not address athletes specifically, so for runners in heavy training it gives a minimum rather than an optimum. Its advice to consult a healthcare provider about persistent sleep problems also fits Došlap's referral logic.
entries.limits: This is a two-page summary of a consensus process, with the full evidence published separately, and it concerns the general adult population rather than athletes. Most of the underlying associations are observational. Evidence strength for the card: high as an authoritative general recommendation, low for athlete-specific thresholds.
entries.strength: high as an authoritative general recommendation, low for athlete-specific thresholds.

A., Phillips, N., Reurink, G., Sadler, R., Grävare Silbernagel, K., Thorborg, K., Wangensteen, A., Wilk, K. E., & Bizzini, M. (2016). 2016 consensus statement on return to sport from the First World Congress in Sports Physical Therapy, Bern. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 50(14), 853–864. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2016-096278

facts.Type: Consensus statement from 17 expert clinicians after the First World Congress in Sports Physical Therapy (Bern, 2015)
facts.Scope: Definitions of return to sport, models for decision-making, and recommendations for clinical practice and research
facts.Main message: Return to sport is a continuum that runs in parallel with rehabilitation, and the decision should be shared among athlete, clinicians and coach, except where the athlete's health is at risk
facts.Version note: The downloaded PDF is the Online First version from May 2016. The final version is 50(14), 853–864.

findings: Return to sport is described as a continuum with three elements: return to participation (active but below the target level), return to sport (back in the sport but not at the desired level) and return to performance (at or above the pre-injury level).
The decision can also be reversed into a removal-from-sport decision. For injuries whose symptoms increase gradually, this usually means reducing or modifying load rather than stopping all activity.

The Strategic Assessment of Risk and Risk Tolerance (StARRT) framework combines tissue health, the stresses the tissue will face and factors that modify how much risk is acceptable, and an athlete is cleared when the assessed risk is below the acceptable threshold.

A biopsychosocial approach is recommended, since psychological readiness, self-efficacy and motivation also influence return to sport, alongside physical tests. Monitoring training load during the transition between stages is suggested, although further research is needed.
The authors state that research evidence to support return-to-sport decisions in clinical practice is scarce.
entries.relevance: This consensus provides the framework for how Došlap can describe the path back after injury. The three-stage continuum maps well onto the app, which could track a runner from return to participation, through return to running, to return to performance. Its emphasis on shared decisions supports the division of roles in which the engine handles load and the physiotherapist decides on clearance, so the AI texts should not declare a runner ready to return. Mapping the continuum onto app stages is my own suggestion.
entries.limits: This is expert consensus built mainly on team sports and clinical experience, and the authors themselves note that research evidence for return-to-sport decisions is scarce. Evidence strength for the card: moderate as a conceptual framework, low for specific criteria.
entries.strength: moderate as a conceptual framework, low for specific criteria.
