International framework for red flags for potential serious spinal pathologies. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy, 50(7), 350–372. https://doi.org/10.2519/jospt.2020.9971

facts.Type: International consensus framework developed for the International Federation of Orthopaedic Manipulative Physical Therapists (IFOMPT)
facts.Method: Expert clinicians' interpretation of the best available evidence, because primary evidence is scarce
facts.Scope: Four serious spinal pathologies presenting as back pain: cauda equina syndrome, spinal fracture, malignancy and spinal infection
facts.Output: A three-step decision tool (consider the evidence, decide the level of concern, choose a referral pathway) with safety netting

findings: Serious spinal pathology is rare in people presenting with back pain (for example, malignancy in well under 1% of cases), yet missing it has serious consequences.
Individual red flags have weak diagnostic value in isolation, and combinations of red flags together with clinical reasoning are more informative.
Signs of cauda equina syndrome, such as a change in bladder or bowel function or altered sensation in the saddle area, require emergency referral.
Where concern is lower, the framework recommends safety netting, meaning the patient is told which symptoms should prompt them to seek help urgently.
entries.relevance: This source supports a red-flag rule in the engine that sits above any training logic. When a user reports symptoms such as bladder or bowel changes, numbness in the saddle area, unexplained weight loss, fever with back pain or pain after significant trauma, the app should stop training advice and direct the user to urgent medical care. It also supports the principle that the app does not diagnose, because the framework itself stresses that the decision belongs to a clinician's reasoning.
entries.limits: The framework is consensus-based rather than derived from new diagnostic studies and concerns back pain, not running injuries in general. Its value for Došlap is therefore as an authoritative basis for safety wording and referral triggers, not as evidence of how often such cases occur among runners.

entries.apa: Geworkian, N., Malon, P., Trojańska, A., Pieńkowska, A., Śliwa, K., Hariasz, N., Pietz, M., & Szymańska, A. (2026). Vitamin D deficiency and risk of overuse musculoskeletal injuries in recreational runners. International Journal of Innovative Technologies in Social Science, 1(49). https://doi.org/10.31435/ijitss.1(49).2026.4858

facts.Type: Narrative review by a group of junior physicians
facts.Journal: International Journal of Innovative Technologies in Social Science, a social science journal. Crossref lists the issue as volume 5, issue 1(49).
facts.Scope: Vitamin D metabolism, its role in bone, muscle and tendon, and the link between vitamin D status and overuse injuries in recreational runners and military recruits
facts.Main message: Low vitamin D is consistently associated with bone stress injuries, whereas evidence for muscle and tendon injuries is limited, and no trials show that correcting it reduces injuries in recreational runners
facts.Note: Not on the original download list

findings: Observational studies in military recruits and athletes consistently associate low serum vitamin D with a higher risk of lower-limb bone stress injuries.
Evidence linking vitamin D to muscle strains, tendinopathies and non-specific musculoskeletal pain is limited and inconsistent.
Low vitamin D is common in endurance athletes, especially in winter, at higher latitudes and in those who train indoors or outside peak sunlight hours.

The main interventional evidence comes from military populations, where calcium and vitamin D supplementation reduced stress fractures in female navy recruits, and the authors caution that this may not transfer directly to recreational runners.
The authors suggest keeping serum vitamin D above 50 nmol/L, and possibly at 75 to 100 nmol/L in runners at higher risk of bone stress injuries, while calling for trials in recreational runners.
entries.relevance: This review supports listing low vitamin D, especially in winter at Czech latitudes, as one of several background factors a physiotherapist or doctor may consider after a bone stress injury. However, testing vitamin D and prescribing supplements are medical decisions, so Došlap's texts should not recommend supplementation or blood levels. The card could at most mention that bone stress injuries have systemic contributing factors that a professional may assess.
entries.limits: This is a narrative review in a journal outside medicine and sport science, its key interventional evidence comes from military recruits, and it contains no new data. Evidence strength for the card: low, and the military trial it relies on is better cited through Warden et al. (2014).
entries.strength: low, and the military trial it relies on is better cited through Warden et al. (2014)

entries.apa: Glisik, N. E., & Frangež, M. (2024). Discrepancies in the prevalence, risk factors, diagnosis, and treatment of stress fractures between long-distance runners and sprinters: A qualitative review of systematic reviews. Exercise and Quality of Life, 16(1), 49–60. https://doi.org/10.31382/eqol.240605

facts.Type: Qualitative review of systematic reviews, led by a medical student at the University of Maribor
facts.Method: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar searched for articles from the previous year only, with 56 articles retained after abstract screening, and no formal quality appraisal described
facts.Scope: Epidemiology, risk factors, diagnosis and treatment of stress fractures in distance runners compared with sprinters
facts.Note: Not on the original download list

findings: Stress fractures in distance runners mainly affect the tibia and metatarsals, whereas in sprinters the toe phalanges are also common.
Reported risk factors include female sex, nutritional deficiencies, biomechanical factors and psychological traits such as perfectionism and fear of failure.

MRI is described as the gold standard for diagnosis, and treatment emphasises rest, a gradual return to activity and addressing underlying risk factors, with surgery reserved for high-risk fractures or non-union.

The review lists high-risk sites that are prone to poor healing, including the anterior tibial shaft, the bases of the second to fourth metatarsals, the great-toe sesamoids, the talus, the navicular and the medial malleolus.

Energy availability and the female athlete triad are highlighted for both distance runners and sprinters. However, the review describes relative energy deficiency in sport as the former name of the female athlete triad, which is inaccurate, since relative energy deficiency is a broader concept that includes the triad.
entries.relevance: The review adds little beyond Warden et al. (2014), which covers the same ground in more depth. Its list of high-risk sites broadly agrees with Warden's, and it could at most serve as a secondary reference for the fact that stress fractures in runners cluster in the tibia and metatarsals.
entries.limits: The search covered only one year of publications and included Google Scholar, no quality appraisal is reported, and one key concept is described inaccurately. Evidence strength for the card: very low.
entries.strength: very low.

entries.apa: Jeukendrup, A. E., Areta, J. L., Van Genechten, L., Langan-Evans, C., Pedlar, C. R., Rodas, G., Sale, C., & Walsh, N. P. (2024). Does relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) syndrome exist? Sports Medicine, 54(11), 2793–2816. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-024-02108-y

facts.Type: Critical narrative review (current opinion)
facts.Focus: The scientific basis of the relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) model as described in the IOC 2023 consensus statement
facts.Main message: The authors do not aim to debunk REDs but argue that the evidence for low energy availability as the single cause of the listed symptoms is weaker than often assumed
facts.Proposal: The Athlete Health and Readiness Checklist (AHaRC), covering eight categories of possible causes
facts.Note: Not on the original download list. It is a critique of, not a substitute for, Mountjoy et al. (2023)

findings: Energy availability cannot be measured accurately enough in the field, so a REDs diagnosis in practice rests on generic symptoms and risk factors.
Most studies show associations rather than causality, observational studies usually last less than seven days, and narrative reviews outnumber original research.
The same symptoms can arise from training load, life stress, mental health problems, disordered eating, other nutritional deficits, poor sleep, infection or an undiagnosed clinical condition.
The authors recommend checking all eight of these categories and involving the relevant experts, rather than starting from the assumption that low energy availability is the cause.
entries.relevance: For Došlap, this source supports a cautious wording policy. The app should not label a user with REDs or any energy-deficiency condition, but persistent fatigue, repeated illness, falling performance, menstrual changes or a bone stress injury can be treated as a combination of signals that warrants referral to a physiotherapist or physician. The eight AHaRC categories also map well onto signals the engine already collects, namely training load, sleep, subjective well-being and illness.
entries.limits: This is an opinion-led review by experienced researchers, and it deliberately challenges a consensus statement, so it should be cited alongside Mountjoy et al. (2023) rather than instead of it. The AHaRC is a proposal that has not been validated.

entries.apa: Silbernagel, K. G., Thomeé, R., Eriksson, B. I., & Karlsson, J. (2007). Continued sports activity, using a pain-monitoring model, during rehabilitation in patients with Achilles tendinopathy: A randomized controlled study. The American Journal of Sports Medicine, 35(6), 897–906. https://doi.org/10.1177/0363546506298279

facts.Design: Randomised controlled trial, level 1 evidence, with follow-up at 6 weeks and 3, 6 and 12 months
facts.Participants: 38 patients with Achilles tendinopathy, about half of them women
facts.Groups: An exercise training group that continued running and jumping guided by a pain-monitoring model, versus an active rest group that avoided Achilles-loading activity for the first 6 weeks. Both followed the same progressive tendon-loading programme for 12 weeks to 6 months.
facts.Pain-monitoring: Pain during activity allowed up to 5 on a 0 to 10
facts.rules: scale, pain after activity allowed up to 5 but settled by the next morning, and pain and stiffness not increasing from week to week
facts.Outcomes: VISA-A-S symptom and function score, pain during hopping, and functional tests
facts.Main result: No difference in the rate of improvement between groups, with both improving significantly

findings: There were no significant differences between the groups in the rate of improvement, and both improved significantly compared with baseline at all follow-ups (p < .01).
The VISA-A-S score rose from 57 to 85 at 12 months in the group that continued running and jumping and from 57 to 91 in the active rest group, a difference that was not statistically significant.
No negative effects of continuing running and jumping were found when activity was guided by the pain-monitoring model.

The continued-activity group showed some better functional results at 6 months (drop jump height and hopping quotient), but the authors caution that the study was powered only for the primary outcome.
The authors conclude that an initial period of rest from pain-provoking activity might not be necessary for Achilles tendinopathy.
entries.relevance: This trial is the key primary evidence for a pain-monitoring rule in Došlap. Its threshold of 5 out of 10 during activity matches the engine's existing referral threshold, and it adds two further conditions, namely that pain should settle by the next morning and should not increase from week to week, which the engine could track through the check-in. Adding these two checks is my own suggestion. However, the rule applies to diagnosed Achilles tendinopathy managed with a physiotherapist, so it does not justify continuing to run with undiagnosed pain or a suspected bone stress injury, and this distinction belongs in the card's limits field.
entries.limits: The trial was small, studied a single condition, and was not powered for its secondary outcomes, so a type II error cannot be ruled out. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for Achilles tendinopathy, low for other conditions.
entries.strength: moderate for Achilles tendinopathy, low for other conditions.

entries.apa: Smith, B. E., Hendrick, P., Smith, T. O., Bateman, M., Moffatt, F., Rathleff, M. S., Selfe, J., & Logan, P. (2017). Should exercises be painful in the management of chronic musculoskeletal pain? A systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 51(23), 1679–1687. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2016-097383

facts.Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (PROSPERO CRD42016038882), using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool and GRADE
facts.Studies included: 9 papers from 7 trials with 385 participants with chronic musculoskeletal pain (low back, shoulder, Achilles and plantar heel), mean age 47, 46% women
facts.Comparison: Exercise in which pain was allowed or encouraged, often up to 5 out of 10, versus pain-free exercise
facts.Main result: A small short-term benefit for pain with painful exercise and no difference in the medium or long term or for function
facts.Version note: The downloaded PDF is the Online First version from July 2017. The final version is 51(23), 1679–1687.

findings: Painful exercise produced a small short-term benefit for pain (effect size −0.27, 95% CI −0.54 to −0.05), based on moderate-quality evidence.
There were no significant differences in pain in the medium or long term, or in function and disability at any time point.
Several trials allowed pain during exercise up to 5 out of 10, and at least one required the pain to settle by the following morning.
The authors conclude that pain during therapeutic exercise for chronic musculoskeletal pain need not be a barrier to successful outcomes.
entries.relevance: This meta-analysis supports the principle behind pain-monitoring approaches, namely that some pain during rehabilitation exercise is acceptable for chronic musculoskeletal conditions. However, it concerns supervised therapeutic exercise in middle-aged patients with chronic pain, not running through new or acute pain. The engine should therefore keep its rule that pain above 5 leads to a referral, and the validator's ban on telling runners to run through pain. The evidence fits best with physiotherapist-guided loading on Došlap's physiotherapy side. This interpretation for Došlap is my own.
entries.limits: The review includes only seven small trials with mixed conditions, none of them in runners or acute injuries, and the benefit it found was small and short-lived. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for the claim that tolerable pain during rehabilitation exercise is not harmful, not applicable to acute pain or bone stress injuries.
entries.strength: moderate for the claim that tolerable pain during rehabilitation exercise is not harmful, not applicable to acute pain or bone stress injuries.

entries.apa: Toczyłowska, A., Muras, M., Hryniuk, W., Kwiecińska, J., Sitkiewicz, J., Bialic, Ł., Mądrzak, L., Korchowiec, M., Chrzanowski, W., & Krzyżanowska, K. (2025). Bone stress injuries in runners: A holistic approach. International Journal of Innovative Technologies in Social Science, 3(47). https://doi.org/10.31435/ijitss.3(47).2025.3471

facts.Type: Narrative literature review by a group of junior physicians
facts.Journal: International Journal of Innovative Technologies in Social Science, a social science journal
facts.Scope: Pathophysiology, risk factors, diagnosis, management and prevention of bone stress injuries in runners
facts.Note: Not on the original download list

findings: Reported risk factors include female sex, low energy availability, low calcium and vitamin D intake, previous stress fracture, low or very high body mass index and sudden changes in the type or intensity of loading.
MRI is described as the diagnostic gold standard after initial plain radiography.

Low-risk injuries are managed conservatively, with a progressive return to running after a period free of pain, whereas high-risk sites (for example, the femoral neck, navicular and anterior tibia) may need prolonged offloading or surgery.

The review summarises a return-to-running scheme that begins at about half of the previous distance and pace once bony tenderness has gone and builds back over three to six weeks, applicable only to low-risk injuries.
entries.relevance: The source adds little beyond Warden et al. (2014). Its one useful point for the engine is the distinction between low-risk and high-risk bone stress injury sites, which supports routing every suspected bone stress injury to a professional rather than offering any self-managed return plan in the app.
entries.limits: The review has no systematic search or quality appraisal, it is published outside the sports medicine literature and it relies on secondary sources. It should not be cited on an evidence card and serves at most as a pointer to the primary literature.

entries.apa: Warden, S. J., Davis, I. S., & Fredericson, M. (2014). Management and prevention of bone stress injuries in long-distance runners. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy, 44(10), 749–765. https://doi.org/10.2519/jospt.2014.5334

facts.Type: Clinical commentary (expert narrative review) by three specialists in bone stress injury
facts.Scope: Pathophysiology, epidemiology, risk factors, diagnosis, classification, management, return to running and prevention of bone stress injuries (BSIs) in long-distance runners
facts.Main message: BSIs lie on a continuum from stress reaction to complete fracture, most heal with modified loading and a gradual, pain-guided return to running, and their high recurrence rate means underlying causes must be addressed

findings: Between one third and two thirds of competitive distance runners report a history of BSI, the 1-year incidence in competitive runners ranges from 4.9% to 21.1%, and 10.3% to 12.6% of runners with a previous BSI sustain another within 1 to 2 years. About half of BSIs in distance runners occur in the tibial shaft.

Typical warning signs are localised bone pain that appears earlier in runs, persists after running, begins to occur during walking, and eventually at rest or at night, together with very localised bony tenderness.

BSIs are classified as low risk (for example posteromedial tibia, fibula, calcaneus and the shafts of the second to fourth metatarsals) or high risk (for example femoral neck, anterior tibia, medial malleolus, navicular, base of the second and fifth metatarsals and great-toe sesamoids), since high-risk sites are prone to delayed healing or complete fracture. Return to sport took about 8.7 weeks for low-risk, low-grade injuries and about 20 weeks for high-risk or high-grade injuries in one cited study.

Return to running after a low-risk BSI begins only once walking is pain-free, and in one programme only after 5 consecutive pain-free days. Progression is strictly symptom-guided, so any BSI pain during or after a session means stopping and returning to the previous stage.

Risk factors include female sex and low energy availability, low calcium or vitamin D, a short history of physical activity, and training changes. In one cited trial, calcium and vitamin D supplementation reduced BSI incidence by 20% in female navy recruits. The authors note that the 10% rule is not generalisable to individual runners, and suggest that increasing step rate by up to 10% can reduce impact loading.
entries.relevance: This paper defines a crucial boundary for the engine's pain logic. Unlike the pain-monitoring model for tendinopathy in Silbernagel et al. (2007), which tolerates pain up to 5 out of 10, return from a bone stress injury is guided by no pain at all. The engine therefore needs to treat localised bone pain, pain that is worse after running, pain during walking and pain at rest or at night as referral triggers regardless of the pain score, and runner-facing texts must never suggest running through such pain. The list of high-risk sites is also useful for how urgently a referral should be framed. Turning these warning signs into check-in triggers is my own suggestion, and the card must avoid anything that reads as a diagnosis.
entries.limits: This is an expert clinical commentary rather than a systematic review, so its return-to-running programmes are based on clinical experience, and much of the epidemiology comes from competitive and military populations. Evidence strength for the card: moderate for the warning signs and the need for referral, low for the specific return-to-running timelines.
entries.strength: moderate for the warning signs and the need for referral, low for the specific return-to-running timelines.

entries.apa: Balsalobre-Fernández, C., Santos-Concejero, J., & Grivas, G. V. (2016). Effects of strength training on running economy in highly trained runners: A systematic review with meta-analysis of controlled trials. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 30(8), 2361–2368. https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0000000000001316

facts.Type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled trials
facts.Sample: 5 studies with 93 competitive middle- and long-distance runners with maximal oxygen uptake above 60 ml/kg/min
facts.Programmes: Mostly low to moderate loads (40 to 70% of one-repetition maximum), 2 to 4 lower-body exercises plus up to 200 jumps and 5 to 10 short sprints, 2 to 3 times per week for 8 to 12 weeks
facts.Version note: The downloaded PDF is the accepted manuscript (Publish Ahead of Print). The reference gives the final issue version.

findings: Strength training had a large beneficial effect on running economy (standardised mean difference −1.42, 95% CI −2.23 to −0.60).
Effective programmes combined resistance exercises with plyometric exercises and did not require very heavy loads or high volumes.
The authors conclude that 2 to 3 sessions per week for 8 to 12 weeks is an appropriate strategy for highly trained runners.
entries.relevance: This meta-analysis gives a quantified basis for a card on running economy and describes a realistic, low-volume programme. For the engine, it supports suggesting short combined sessions of strength and jumping exercises rather than long gym sessions.
entries.limits: Only five small studies were pooled, all in highly trained runners, so the large effect may not transfer to recreational users. The confidence interval is wide. Running economy is a laboratory marker and does not directly measure race performance or injury risk.

entries.apa: Blagrove, R. C., Howatson, G., & Hayes, P. R. (2018). Effects of strength training on the physiological determinants of middle- and long-distance running performance: A systematic review. Sports Medicine, 48(5), 1117–1149. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-017-0835-7

facts.Type: Systematic review without meta-analysis, study quality rated with the PEDro scale
facts.Sample: 24 controlled studies of middle- and long-distance runners with at least six months of running experience and a running-only control group
facts.Interventions: Heavy resistance training, explosive resistance training and plyometric training lasting at least four weeks
facts.Outcomes: Running economy, time-trial performance (1.5 to 10 km), sprint speed, maximal oxygen uptake, blood lactate and body composition

findings: Running economy was measured in 20 studies and generally improved by 2 to 8% compared with running-only control groups, although not in every study.
Time-trial performance over 1.5 to 10 km and sprint speed also tended to improve, whereas maximal oxygen uptake, blood lactate markers and body composition were typically unaffected.
Adding strength training did not harm aerobic markers or body composition, which addresses the common concern among runners that lifting makes them heavier or slower.

Most successful programmes used two to three sessions per week for 6 to 14 weeks, a weak link between session frequency and running-economy gains suggested that two sessions per week is likely sufficient, and the authors advise a gap of more than three hours after high-intensity running before a strength session.
entries.relevance: This review supports a performance card stating that two strength sessions per week can make running more economical without adding body mass. The advice on separating hard running and strength work by several hours, or placing them on different days, can inform how the engine schedules strength sessions around key runs.
entries.limits: Study quality was moderate (PEDro 4 to 6), samples were small and findings were not always consistent. Most participants were trained or well-trained runners, so the size of the benefit for recreational runners is uncertain. The review does not address injury prevention.

entries.apa: Khan, S. (2026). Warm-up programs as a key strategy for injury prevention in youth sports [Editorial]. The Therapist (Journal of Therapies & Rehabilitation Sciences), 7(1), 1–2. https://doi.org/10.54393/tt.v7i01.302

facts.Type: Two-page editorial
facts.Main message: Structured warm-up programmes reduce sports injuries in youth, and compliance determines how large the effect is
facts.Note: Not on the original download list

findings: The editorial cites a meta-analysis by Ding et al. of 15 studies with more than 21,500 children and adolescents, reporting about a 36% reduction in sports injuries with warm-up programmes.
Programmes built on neuromuscular control, balance and strength were the most effective.
Consistent, structured implementation was a key moderator of the effect.
entries.relevance: The editorial is of marginal use because Došlap targets adult runners. Its main value is as a pointer to the Ding et al. meta-analysis, and it is consistent with Lauersen et al. (2014) in showing that strength and neuromuscular content, rather than stretching, drives the preventive effect.
entries.limits: An editorial with no original data, published in a small journal, and focused on youth team sports. It should not be cited on an evidence card. If a warm-up card is wanted, the underlying meta-analysis should be obtained instead.

entries.apa: Lauersen, J. B., Bertelsen, D. M., & Andersen, L. B. (2014). The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 48(11), 871–877. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2013-092538

facts.Type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
facts.Sample: 25 trials with 26,610 participants and 3,464 injuries across a range of sports, mostly team sports and military populations
facts.Interventions: Stretching, proprioception (balance) training, strength training and programmes combining several exercise types
facts.Outcome: Risk of sports injury expressed as relative risk (RR), analysed for acute and overuse injuries separately

findings: Across all trials, exercise interventions reduced sports injuries by about a third (RR 0.632).
Strength training showed the largest effect (RR 0.315, 95% CI 0.207–0.480, four trials, I² = 0%), which corresponds to roughly a two-thirds reduction in injuries.
Proprioception training (RR 0.550) and multi-component programmes (RR 0.655) were also protective, whereas stretching had no effect (RR 0.963, not significant).
Both overuse injuries (RR 0.527) and acute injuries (RR 0.647) were reduced, and the authors conclude that overuse injuries can be almost halved.
entries.relevance: This is the core source for a strength-training evidence card. It supports a plain-Czech claim that regular strength training lowers the risk of injury and that stretching alone does not, and it can justify a nudge when a runner logs no strength sessions over several weeks. Because the source does not define a dose for runners, the engine should recommend strength work in general terms and leave the specific programme to the physiotherapist.
entries.limits: The strength-training estimate rests on only four trials, none of them in recreational runners, and the included populations are mostly soldiers and team-sport athletes. Compliance was reported inconsistently. The evidence is strong for the general message that exercise-based prevention works, but moderate for transferring the effect size to runners.

entries.apa: Llanos-Lagos, C., Ramirez-Campillo, R., Moran, J., & Sáez de Villarreal, E. (2024). The effect of strength training methods on middle-distance and long-distance runners' athletic performance: A systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Medicine, 54(7), 1801–1833. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-024-02018-z

facts.Type: Systematic review with meta-analysis, certainty of evidence rated with GRADE
facts.Sample: 38 randomised and non-randomised controlled studies with 894 moderately to highly trained runners
facts.Interventions: High-load (at least 80% of one-repetition maximum), submaximal-load (40 to 79%), plyometric and combined strength training, 6 to 40 weeks, 1 to 4 sessions per week
facts.Outcomes: Time-trial and time-to-exhaustion performance, maximal oxygen uptake, velocity at maximal oxygen uptake, maximum metabolic steady state and sprint capacity
facts.Note: Not on the original download list

findings: High-load strength training had a moderate effect on running performance (effect size −0.469), and combining two or more methods had a large effect (effect size −1.035).
Plyometric training alone did not reach significance (effect size −0.210, p = 0.064).
No method improved maximal oxygen uptake, velocity at maximal oxygen uptake, maximum metabolic steady state or sprint capacity.
Sex, age, performance level, strength-training experience and programme length did not moderate the effects, and the certainty of evidence was very low to moderate.
entries.relevance: This is the most recent and largest meta-analysis in the section. It supports a card stating that heavy strength training, ideally combined with other methods such as jumps, can improve race times, and that the benefit applies across runner levels. Together with Blagrove et al. (2018), it suggests the effect works through running economy and neuromuscular factors rather than aerobic capacity.
entries.limits: Certainty of evidence was low to moderate, and several analyses contained few studies. Performance outcomes were short time trials and laboratory tests, so benefits for marathon or trail distances are extrapolated. The review does not address injury.

entries.apa: Rønnestad, B. R., & Mujika, I. (2014). Optimizing strength training for running and cycling endurance performance: A review. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, 24(4), 603–612. https://doi.org/10.1111/sms.12104

facts.Type: Narrative review by two leading researchers in concurrent training
facts.Focus: Effects of heavy and explosive strength training added to endurance training, with practical programming advice
facts.Version note: The downloaded PDF is the accepted manuscript (2013). The reference gives the final issue version.

findings: In runners, both heavy and explosive strength training improved running economy and running performance, whereas cycling benefited mainly from heavy strength training.
No negative effects of adding strength training to an endurance programme were reported.

The authors recommend two sessions per week for about 12 weeks, 2 to 3 sets of 4 to 10 repetition-maximum loads with 2 to 3 minutes of rest, and developing proper technique with lighter loads before lifting heavy.

About one low-volume, high-intensity session per week appears to maintain strength gains during the competitive season, and runners should expect heavy, sore legs in the first two to three weeks and reduce endurance training at that point.
entries.relevance: This review provides the most concrete programming guidance in the section. It supports two engine behaviours, namely a build phase with two strength sessions per week and a maintenance phase with one session per week during race preparation, and a warning card that leg soreness is common in the first weeks of a new strength programme.
entries.limits: This is a narrative review without a systematic search, and the recommendations are based on a small number of studies in well-trained athletes. The loading advice is expert opinion informed by evidence rather than a tested prescription for recreational runners.

entries.apa: Yismaw, A. S., Wondem, D. A., Wubale, A. A., & Belay, A. T. (2026). Effect of concurrent training on middle-distance running performances in trained athletes. Pamukkale Journal of Sport Sciences. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.54141/psbd.1752868

facts.Design: Quasi-experimental pre-test and post-test study
facts.Participants: 30 trained adolescent middle-distance runners in Ethiopia (mean age 17.3 years), 10 per group
facts.Groups: Endurance only, strength only and concurrent (endurance plus strength) training, three sessions per week for 12 weeks
facts.Outcomes: Squats, push-ups, estimated maximal oxygen uptake (Cooper test) and 2-km time trial
facts.Note: Not on the original download list

findings: The concurrent group improved more than the endurance-only group in all measures, including the 2-km time trial.
The strength-only group gained most in muscular endurance but did not improve its 2-km time.
The authors themselves warn that the very large effect sizes are likely inflated by the small, homogeneous sample.
entries.relevance: The study is consistent with the reviews in this section but adds nothing that they do not already establish. It should not be used on an evidence card.
entries.limits: Very small sample, adolescent athletes, group allocation by baseline performance rather than randomisation, field-estimated outcomes and implausibly large effects. Evidence strength is weak.
